Official report on the CIA Orientation Course (Fourth Group) covers the program of 2 to 5 October 1951, 0900 to 1200 each day, in the Department of Agriculture Auditorium. The move to that hall was made to escape the noise of the temporary building used before. It also gained seats after a four month gap since the third course. The hall pleased the office: handy to most CIA offices, and with good acoustics, the report states.

The course substance was woven around the four part pattern of the series. Attendance is fixed by matching the first and final registration slips, at 535. Appreciation singles out a departing staff member whose constant help cut the task of staging the program to a bearable size. The report closes by hoping course dates will be fixed, so other offices can plan around them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100070017-0:
Summary report on the opening phase of the Human Resources Program in the Technical Services Staff, sent by the Chief, Management Training Division. Sessions were held in April with groups of supervisors, branch chiefs among them, and each group got the same outline material apart from a first page summing up its own earlier talks. The scan is partly garbled, though the argument reads clearly.

Program thinking rests on the idea that gains made by business and industry in handling people can serve the Agency too. Management is treated as work done through others, so growing people is part of the job. Teamwork and a sense of taking part in choices are stressed. The report finds able, keen staff, yet a wide sense that coordination across the staff was lacking.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100080016-0:
Attachment A lists directors of area and regional programs at American universities, naming the school, the program, and the person then holding the post. Entries run in alphabetical order by institution. California at Berkeley appears with its institutes for Slavic studies, East Asiatic studies, and international relations, and Columbia follows with Russian, East Asian, Pakistan, and Israeli studies centers.

Later pages cover Cornell and its China and Southeast Asia programs, Harvard and its Russian Research Center and China program, and Michigan, Princeton, and other schools. Some entries note that no holder was indicated, or that a post was unknown at the time. The list reads as a contact and reference sheet for area study centers across the country, giving program titles beside the scholars who directed them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030023-0:
Central Intelligence Agency regulation on overseas payments. It covers foreign area differentials and allowances. It also covers territorial payments. The text runs to many pages of rules. Its aim is fair terms for staff abroad. Terms overseas should sit close to terms in Washington. Staff in foreign countries are covered. Staff in United States territories are covered too.

Federal rules are brought in by reference. State Department rules govern foreign post differentials. State rules also govern foreign area allowances. Civil Service Commission rules govern territorial payments. Key terms are defined early in the text. Foreign area and territorial area both get meanings. Later rules set a firm cap. A cost-of-living payment plus a differential cannot pass twenty-five percent. That cap is figured on base pay. Unclassified posts get their own rule.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020034-0:
Sanitized bundle of interim reports and related memos. Names of people are redacted throughout. A memo dated 17 June 1953 leads the file. It forwards interim evaluations of three men. The men were in intensive Arabic training. Twenty class hours a week went to spoken Arabic. The Damascus dialect was the one taught. Six more hours went to seminars. Those covered intercultural relations and the Near East.

Group morale is praised as extremely high. Hard work and steady focus are noted. A later memo speaks to Agency recruiters. It dates from 10 August 1953. Assessment tests now screened out many candidates. Perhaps half of them failed to pass. Recruiters placed fewer people as a result. Rejected candidates placed elsewhere would be followed. Their careers would test how sound the screening was. Other pages sketch the recruit sought. Stability, realism, and love of country are stressed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100040014-0:
Table of contents for a bound set of Office of Training notices. Notices from 1952 are listed first. Subjects include use of Agency motor pool facilities. Parking permits and a security officer posting appear. Purchase requisitions and charity drives are listed too. Personnel assignments fill many entries. A promotion panel notice appears near the end.

Notices from 1953 follow in the same list. The notices themselves fill the rest of the file. One rescinds an earlier personnel board notice. That notice, number 25-52, dates from 15 November 1952. It sets up a Training (Special) promotion panel. Matthew Baird signed as Director of Training. Other notices cover stand-by duty rosters. Courier service and leave schedules also appear. Classified material left in empty rooms gets a warning. Library services for courses are announced as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100060003-0:
Agenda and record for group meeting number two. Agency training officers of the plans directorate attended. Communications staff attended the meeting as well. It sat on Wednesday 8 July 1953. The time was 2:30 in the afternoon. Training materials for overseas use headed the agenda. Area training and budget follow-up followed.

A memorandum for the record came a day later. It dates from 9 July 1953. Training materials were discussed at the request of one office. A draft regulation had been prepared for the meeting. Materials were to flow through a training committee. Release to foreign services was carved out of the paper. A separate paper on that point was in preparation. Control after release worried the group. Once materials left, no guarantee of control remained. Communications materials were exempted from the paper.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56s00490a000700090018-0:
Soviet Intelligence Summary, serial SIS 50-17, dated 25 April 1950. The Department of the Navy issued the summary. The Chief of Naval Operations office, Op-32, stands behind it. Strict handling warnings open the text. Only indoctrinated staff may read the summary. Communications intelligence rules govern its use. No action may risk revealing the source.

A long distribution list follows the warnings. Naval, joint staff, and State Department readers are named. The body reports on Soviet naval matters. One passage weighs four naval units and their designations. Only a sighting would settle what names they used. Another passage assesses a shipyard. The summary reports it was probably set up early in 1943. It had no dry dock of its own. It used dry dock space in a merchant fleet yard. Repair and modernization work on ships is reported there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000120049-0:
Amendment number one to contract number FS-99. The amendment is dated 24 April 1956. Hycon Manufacturing Company of Pasadena is the contractor. Training of more personnel is its purpose. The Changes clause of the contract gives the authority. An old appendix is deleted by the amendment. A new appendix of the same date replaces it.

New schedule text sets the training in detail. Three teams of nine men each are required. They will serve as field service teams overseas. Their job is servicing and maintaining basic equipment. One roving field engineer is added as well. The Agency provides the basic equipment for training. Training places are also government provided. That work abroad sits under a separate contract. Billing terms follow in the amendment. A monthly billing figure of 1,300 dollars appears. A total cap is stated for the billings. All other contract terms stay unchanged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000130165-0:
Memorandum dated 30 May from the Project Communications Officer. It went to the Agency Project Personnel Officer. A communications table of organization is its subject. The table attached was submitted for approval. Staffing stands above the first staffing level. That growth rests on operational experience. It also rests on the need to keep pace. The table will grow again as requirements grow.

Technical representation gets a firm caution. Two named services supply that representation. Their people must not replace communications personnel. They must not serve as an addition either. That point is stated plainly in the memo. The table itself lists communications posts. Specialists, an electronics engineer, and a clerk-typist appear. Maintenance posts are listed in the table too. Cryptographic technicians fill many of the rows. Their grade levels run in a narrow band.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100080004-0:
Memorandum dated 27 May 1951 to the CIA Career Service Board. Policies governing training at non-CIA facilities form the subject. Training should tie directly to career service. A person must declare a career intention first. Qualifications must show capability for the training goal. The projected training must benefit the Agency. It may raise skill in the current assignment. It may prepare the person for a greater one.

Use of the person after training must be settled. That use must be determined before training starts. Fixed-quota places are filled on a competitive basis. Agency interest as a whole comes first there. Career boards recommend each candidate for training. The office head or staff chief must approve. Requests need endorsement to be considered at all. The Director of Training gives the final consideration. These rules bind selection from the start.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100110025-0:
General comments common to four field offices. The comments come from a survey of those offices. Teletype message files open the list of comments. All copies were kept indefinitely by the offices. Little use is made of material over thirty days old. Almost no use is made of sixty-day material. Destruction after sixty days is recommended instead. Logs would cover the occasional need for old items.

Repeat transmission from Agency headquarters could supply old material. Obsolete and little-used holdings fill the offices too. Working papers and other offices' reports are named. Staff did not know what could be destroyed. That ignorance built the file situation, it states. A records management publication was pending at the time. A vigorous program to cut files is urged. Critical vault space would be conserved by it. Salary check signing is called an obsolete practice. Fund mixing caused account discrepancies in one office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200120023-0:
Electrical business machines survey prepared for a House committee. The House Appropriations Committee is the named audience. Machine Division of OCD at the Agency supplied the data. Units rented or owned are listed at 30 June 1953. IBM punches numbered twenty-five in the table. Utilization for them reads fifty-nine percent. Verifiers numbered thirteen at sixty-six percent.

Collators numbered nine and sorters eleven in the count. Sorter utilization reads seventy-seven percent there. One statistical machine and four tabulators appear. Three reproducers and one gang punch follow. Three interpreters close the standard machine list. An electronic scanner and receiver appear separately. Operating personnel took 46.7 man years that year. Supporting personnel took 27.8 man years more. Notes explain peak period operations for OCD divisions. Crash information demands can arrive at any time. Equipment stays available to all divisions for that reason. Indexing of intelligence material is called unique.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100020001-0:
CIA redraft of a draft foreign information program paper. Draft number fifteen is the base text here. Overt psychological warfare planning rides with it. Foreign information in peace is a permanent instrument. Psychological warfare in emergency or war is equally permanent. Both must aim continuously at national aims. Department and agency activities form the essential elements.

Those activities form the essential nucleus for warfare too. Continuity between peace and war plans is the goal. Strengthening and coordination of activities is sought. The Secretary of State bears defined responsibility. Policy for a national foreign information program is his. Influencing foreign attitudes favorably is its purpose. All government foreign information activities fall under it. Wartime plans are treated in the later text. Preparations for national emergency are recommended there. Initial stages of war are covered by the plans. Coordination with joint war plans is continuous.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100140026-0:
Bundle of topic papers from an overseas administrative activity. Travel data sheets lead the papers in this copy. Effective 1 February 1953, vouchers change handling. Travel data sheets would be furnished per traveler. About thirty individuals arrived from headquarters since. Dates between February and 16 April 1953 are given. No travel data sheets have been received there.

Computations proceed by discussion and other documentation meanwhile. Forwarding of sheets is the indicated action onward. Tour length forms the next topic paper. Home leave for military personnel is not authorized. Agency overseas tours run two years generally. Assignments to the Agency run three years instead. Extension by an additional year can be agreed. Support payment systems close the bundle topics. Direct cash payment is one option weighed. Army facilities would be bypassed under it. A reimbursement procedure is a second option. Cost factors per annum form a third. Funds would transfer to the Army in Washington.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150089-0:
Notes as a basis for discussion of Agency functions. Duties of the Agency share the title focus. The intelligence problem in the United States opens it. The Agency is largely an outgrowth of war years. World War II is that shaping experience named. Prewar government was not without intelligence though. State maintained a wide information gathering service.

Army and Navy maintained their own systems too. Other departments collected and produced intelligence on their own. Yet no joined system existed in that era. On hand sources went poorly used as well. No central agency coordinated collection and production. Best intelligence lacked assembly into national estimates. Foreign policy shaping needed those estimates badly. Power to coordinate is examined in later sections. The act grants no free-standing coordinating power. Advice passes to the National Security Council. Final charge for policies vests there instead. Advising the Council is a main duty.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100200047-0: Minutes of an Agency Liaison Security Committee meeting, 2 February 1948. Minutes of the 26 January meeting were approved. Wider use of a cover address was discussed. Permission should be obtained in each case, the committee held. State Department post reports were arranged for next. Army and Navy post reports were arranged alongside. The files sit in an Overseas Section for reference. Control of issuances to the field was deferred. Security problems in outside training courses were also discussed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100210118-0:
Memo dated 29 July 1947 on advice board steps. The chief received it through a middle office. Whether two sections are lawful is the question posed. A 25 July 1947 memo holds those sections. Section eight covers handing out of advice. An advice board member hands them out for a vote. Section two covers advice forwarded. Backing of one other member triggers forwarding.

The chief must forward such advice. His comments go with them to the Authority. Other members' comments go with them as well. On section eight alone no legal question stands. Board functions need member weighing of advice. Sections two and three raise the problem. Read word for word they would force the chief. Advice he might disagree with would go up. Two backing members could force that result. Duties of the chief need review. Department heads sit in a dual capacity there. As board members their focus is the chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220009-0:
Dated 8 October 1953, a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence asks what laws should be sought on the shape of the CIA Career Staff and its service program. A task force prepared the study, while noting that members backed its broad line more than every single argument. Agency rules already split staff into career and temporary groups. Rules also set up a Career Service Board and boards inside each part of the Agency.

From that base, the study tests what a law should add on structure, entry, and control of the career service. It treats the board system as the frame through which career policy runs. Readers get an early plan for turning a loose set of long-term staff into a named, ordered service with its own governing boards.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220054-0:
On 26 June 1953 the Executive Secretary of the CIA Career Service Board sent its chairman a list of matters bearing on a planned law program. Items fall into three groups: points already raised in a CIA notice, actions already under way, and open problems needing a choice. Some problems might be solved by law, while others could be settled by policy under laws already in force. The list ranges from added benefits for staff hurt on duty to pay and grade rises.

Each item carries a short note on what has been done so far, and several notes record that little or nothing had moved. Read as a working agenda, the memorandum shows which parts of career policy staff thought Congress had to fix. It also shows how much of the program still sat at the idea stage in mid-1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050005-0:
Senate bill S. 3830 of the 81st Congress, brought in by Mr. Frear on 26 June 1950, would set a hiring path for the competitive civil service. It was read twice and sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The short title given in the text is the Federal Personnel Recruitment Act of 1950. Its stated aim is choice of staff by open contest and merit.

Early clauses fix what the word department covers across the federal government and the District of Columbia. Later parts build the machinery for tests, lists, and appointments under the Civil Service Act. The bill is the Senate twin of a House measure in the same file, and it shows Congress working on hiring rules in full statutory detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060086-0:
Army Regulation Number 35-1495, issued in Washington on 23 February 1948, sets the finance rules for parachute pay. A contents list runs from the rating itself through duty, end of duty, physical demands, certificates, and accidents. The opening clause covers Army officers, warrant officers, and enlisted men for whom jumping is a core part of duty. Those in flying-pay status are left out.

Pay is fixed at one hundred dollars a month for officers and warrant officers, with a lower rate for enlisted men. The text cites the act of 16 June 1942, as changed in 1944, and dates the rules from 1 June 1942. Later clauses work through how jumps in one month can cover months around it. For an agency with airborne work in its past, the regulation fixed who earned the extra pay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090001-0:
Public Law 724 of the 79th Congress, printed as Chapter 957 from H.R. 6967, carries the full text of the Foreign Service Act of 1946. Its stated aim is to improve, strengthen, and expand the Foreign Service of the United States. The act also gathers and revises the older laws on how that service is run. Title I gives the short title, the goals set by Congress, and the meanings of terms used through the act.

Congress declares that officers and staff should stand broadly for the American people and know current American life well. Later titles work through grades, pay, postings, and the running of the service in detail. Kept in Agency files, the act mattered because CIA people served beside, and sometimes inside, the Foreign Service frame it built.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090074-0:
Explanatory notes, in a draft dated 9 June 1947, walk through a proposed bill section by section and gloss the statutes each part cites. One note deals with retired military officers, for whom no statute is cited in the bill. Another explains how the Foreign Service Act of 1946 lets officers be assigned to other agencies, and why a clear exception was written in. The aim is to keep the standing of an officer lent outside his own service free from doubt.

Further notes tackle the bans on drawing two salaries from public funds. Cited parts of Title 5 set limits where combined pay passes a fixed sum, with exceptions the bill needs. The scan is rough, yet the draft's job is clear: show drafters what each borrowed law would do.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400170002-0:
An outline dated April 1951, marked OGC-Navy, lists the laws and directives behind defence mobilisation and emergency powers. It opens with Second World War measures: the limited emergency proclamation of 8 September 1939 and the unlimited one of 27 May 1941. The cessation of hostilities at the end of 1946 and a 1947 law ending certain war powers follow. Statute references and dates anchor each entry.

First and Second War Powers Acts are broken into their titles, from coordination of bureaus to war contracts, priorities, and requisition powers. Price control and facility purchase laws appear in their turn. The outline is a lawyer's map of what emergency law existed, what had lapsed, and what a new mobilisation could reach for.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400170011-0:
Gathered in one survey are the provisions of law that would become operative when the President proclaimed a national emergency. The opening group treats clauses affected by the joint resolution of 25 July 1947, which closed the state of war and the emergencies then standing. Each entry gives the act's date and statute page, then the words that set the power loose. Control of an airfield at Tucson, leased from the city, is one such case.

A land exchange near Yuma, with War Department control of an airfield in an emergency, follows the same pattern. So does a 1925 clause guarding use of the Hoboken Manufacturers' Railroad. The document is a reference sweep of dormant powers, built so officials could see the legal ground shift in advance of any crisis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180119-0:
Travel orders come in three basic kinds, and a General Counsel paper of 20 March explains when each kind is used and what follows from the choice. Permanent change of station orders move a worker's headquarters from one place to another for good. In foreign travel they can also fix a person's first post of duty abroad. Temporary duty orders send a worker away from headquarters for a short spell.

Home leave stands as the third kind, for trips earned by overseas service. Each kind carries its own rules on pay, family movement, and goods. Picking the wrong form could change what the government owed the traveller. The paper was written at the request of an Assistant Deputy Director for Administration who wanted the common cases set out plainly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050004-0:
S. 352, brought into the Senate on 11 January 1951 by Mr. Johnston of South Carolina, aims to simplify and gather the laws on pay from two government jobs at once. It was read twice and sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The opening rule is broad: unless a law clearly allows it, a person paid from one federal office may not draw pay from another. An exception runs only so far as the two sums together stay under a set cap.

District of Columbia posts and government-owned companies are swept into the same rule. Later clauses sort out classes of staff, retired pay, and cases where double service is allowed. The bill shows the dual-pay tangle Congress kept returning to in this period.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500070002-0:
A blank Personal Service Contract form sets out the terms on which the Agency took on a single contractor's work. Header fields name the type of service and employment, the length of the contract, and the rate of pay. Check boxes mark a consultant or expert, working part-time or for a short spell. Pay may run per day of service or per diem for hours actually worked. Space is left for the total cost expected.

Further boxes record whether the contractor is a retired civilian employee or a retired officer of the Armed Services. Date of appointment papers and the nature of the services follow. A justification block for the contract is printed below the signature lines. The form shows the paper shape of buying one person's skill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140004-0:
Public Law 810 of the 80th Congress, Chapter 708 from H.R. 2744, bears the short title Army and Air Force Vitalization and Retirement Equalization Act of 1948. It covers removal of Regular Army and Regular Air Force officers from the active list. It also covers retirement of officers, warrant officers, and enlisted men of those services. Reserve members of the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard gain retirement benefits under it.

Title I, on elimination, lets each service secretary remove a commissioned officer for causes he finds satisfactory, in the manner the act prescribes. Later titles work through retirement ages, pay, and the rights of those removed. The act evened the terms between the ground and air services just after the Air Force stood alone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140013-0:
Your Retirement System, a Civil Service Commission booklet, answers questions on the federal civil service retirement law in a set order. Contents run from coverage and employee contributions to eligibility and annuity sums. Refunds and redeposits get their own part, and a miscellaneous part and appendix close the book. Early answers list who is shut out by executive order: staff on temporary appointments of a year or less head the list.

Contract and fee-basis staff, and some paid only when actually employed, are also outside. Later answers explain how the order of 1 May 1942 changed the ground for temporary staff. Worked examples show how an annuity is figured. For personnel offices, this was the standard handout given to any worker who asked.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040018-0:
Mr. Aiken's report of 26 May 1948, Report Number 1413, backs S. 2754 under the heading Federal Property Act of 1948. The Senate Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments had weighed government property management. It reports the bill, meant to reorganise and simplify buying, use, and disposal of government property, and urges passage. Historical background leads the argument.

A sound property system had been sought since a 1943 House bill tried to build one. That effort was overtaken by war surplus machinery with a short life, set to end with the cessation of hostilities. A presidential message of 5 March 1948 is brought into the account. This 1948 report is the direct forerunner of the act passed the next year under a longer name.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000060007-0:
Salary Table Number 22 of the General Accounting Office, issued 25 July 1945, covers the executive branch from 1 July 1945. A forty-hour week heads the title. The tables replace those in force after 30 June 1945. They serve staff paid by the year, through the officers who make up and certify the payrolls.

Period figures for a full two weeks are given by rate under the Federal Employees Pay Act of 1945. Hourly and daily rates stand beside them. Tax deductions rest on the Individual Income Tax Act of 1944, cited at 58 Stat. 250. Notes then state what a payroll or voucher must show for audit. Dated weeks before the war's end, the table paid a government still at full war strength.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000080014-0:
Provisions presenting the enemy problem are listed in a legal paper dated 15 January 1952. The problem is words: statutes speak of the enemy, or of things captured by the enemy, in terms clear in war but clouded in peace. The task is to fix what such words mean where a provision runs on past the end of a state of war. Item 263 heads the visible list, the War Hazards Compensation Act.

That act, cited at 42 U.S.C. 1701 and following, pays for death or injury of certain United States and contractor staff from a war-risk hazard. A note under it flags the public use of the United States or its agents, at 42 U.S.C. 1651(b). Each later item gets the same treatment: cite, summary, and the enemy wording that troubles the lawyers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020037-0:
General military rights, apart from any single base or facility, form the subject of a summary on what executive agreements should secure. Physical needs of operating forces in a given area are only half the picture, the opening argues. Agreements, whether with one country or many, must also carry set features that let them be carried out. Past deals with several countries give a fairly standard pattern for drafting such items.

Standard wording is called desirable wherever it can be kept. Yet each country tends to seek departures on a few points of its own. Inside NATO, much progress toward common terms is noted, including jurisdiction over military personnel. The summary reads as drafting guidance for the lawyers who wrote status arrangements for American forces abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100050025-0:
An official report of the UNESCO Committee of Copyright Experts, meeting in Washington from 23 October to 4 November 1950, fills this file copy. UNESCO invited the meeting, and the Library of Congress with the United States Copyright Office hosted it in the Old House Office Building. Fifteen experts from various countries took part. The head of UNESCO's Copyright Division, and delegates of the Berne Union and the Pan-American Union, sat with them, along with advisers and observers.

A list of those present is annexed. The report records the talks toward a fresh universal copyright convention, meant to bridge the Berne and Pan-American systems. Sessions worked through national treatment, translation rights, and terms of protection. The text was issued as an appendix to the Library of Congress Information Bulletin of 6 November 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030008-0:
Publications supplied to United States government agencies at home, distributed through the New York Maritime Association, are listed in a priced table. Subscribers are named one by one: the Eastern Sea Frontier office on Church Street in New York, an operation control officer at Norfolk, and the Naval Supply Center's freight terminal there. Each entry gives the publication mark, copies taken, annual subscription in dollars, and expiry date.

Refunds are shown at the rate paid and at a higher rate with a percentage added. The Hydrographic Office in Washington and the Military Sea Transportation Service take the largest copy counts in the visible list. Dates in 1953 mark when subscriptions fell due. The table shows Lloyd's shipping publications woven into daily naval staff work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030017-0:
A resume of budgetary analysis of intelligence programs, planned by Bureau of the Budget staff, records a talk given on Tuesday 17 November 1953. Robert Macy, chief of the Bureau's International Division, presented it to the Intelligence Advisory Committee. The talk is offered as a useful addition to the community's habit of critical self-review. Hearings the past spring showed Congress wanted proof that intelligence work across the government was being screened inside the executive branch.

Until then, Bureau officials could not discuss in detail how one agency's work bore on another's. The analysis opens that comparison: programs, costs, and overlaps across the intelligence community. The paper is marked restricted, and it captures the moment systematic budget review first reached secret work as a whole.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030071-0:
A secret draft memorandum of 19 April 1951 from the Director of Central Intelligence proposes an Economic Intelligence Committee to the Intelligence Advisory Committee. It partly answers a National Security Council memorandum of 3 March 1950, sent by the Council's Executive Secretary. That paper required a study of economic security intelligence needs and facilities across the government. A full plan for meeting foreign economic intelligence needs was the end in view.

The problem section starts with a count: some twenty-four agencies then collected and analysed foreign economic data on a regular basis. Their data, facilities, and purposes varied widely. The draft argues for joined effort under one committee. An appendix holds the Council paper that set the task in motion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300070012-0:
An air transport services agreement between the United States and the Union of Burma was signed at Rangoon on 28 September 1949 and took force the same day. The State Department printed it as Publication 3691 in 1950, priced at five cents. A contents page shows the agreement itself followed by an annex. Both governments state their wish to put air services between their territories on a settled footing.

Articles cover the grant of routes, the naming of airlines, and the charges and rules each side applies. The annex sets the actual routes to be flown. Such post-war air agreements built the map of international flying piece by piece. This copy sat in a legal file where treaty texts were kept for the questions they answered about rights abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300360029-0:
An untitled report sums up a year of work by the Interdepartmental Federal Tort Claims Committee. Problems had piled up since the committee last met on 10 July 1947. A fresh meeting was called for 14 May 1951, and notices went to every agency with a stake in running the Federal Tort Claims Act. Sessions followed on 22 June, 10 July, 1 August, 5 and 19 September, and 26 November 1951.

Agencies represented are listed with the men who sat for them, from the General Accounting Office and the Army and Navy Departments to the Post Office and Public Housing Administration. The report records each action the committee took across those meetings. Tort claims against the government needed one shared handling, and this committee was the table where agencies agreed it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100010031-0:
Instruction from the Department of State to the American embassy in Japan concerns revision of Article IV of the Administrative Agreement. It is dated with reference to an April 1953 note from the Japanese foreign ministry, as the NATO status of forces agreement was about to take effect. Draft enclosures are sent with it: a note to the Japanese minister, draft changes to the Japanese draft protocol, and proposals for official minutes.

Two United States proposals are flagged as likely to cause difficulty. One adds a paragraph on suspension in the event of hostilities. The embassy is told it would not let the United States restore an exclusive jurisdiction setup by its own act alone. The other concerns Japan waiving its primary right to exercise jurisdiction. Later pages work through wording changes in the protocol, point by point, to match the NATO agreement.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200160016-0:
Standard Form number 8, October 1954, Department of Labor Regulation 609.2, is a Notice to Separated Federal Employee under the unemployment compensation program. The form tells the former employee to keep it, since its facts will help settle rights to compensation. It lists what to take to the nearest public employment office to file a claim.

Items to bring are the form itself, any such forms received in the past twenty four months, the social security card, and the official notice of separation, such as Standard Form 50. A box gives the office where payroll records are kept, with a sample Washington address. Attached forms request wage and separation facts from the agency, ask whether the person performed federal service, and record base period wage figures for a state.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130117-0:
Note dated 11 April 1956, titled Transfer of Control of Langley Property, records the state of talks on land at the Langley site, in a partly garbled scan. The Bureau of Public Roads had ended its claim to part of the Langley site. The National Park Service had shown willingness to release the access road running through the site. Counsel saw no bar to the main transfer.

Two legal paths are weighed. One proceeds under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, which lets the Administrator of General Services transfer surplus property between agencies. The other concerns a parcel of about eighteen acres, with a question whether it was ever set aside for national forest or national park purposes. The note stresses that inquiries were for information only, no transfer was yet to be started, and lists factors to weigh.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130153-0:
Memorandum for the record dated 20 March 1956, titled CIA Building: Discussions with Mr. Nolen and Mr. Massey, records talks held on 19 March with the director of the National Capital Planning Commission and with the Fairfax County Executive, in their own offices. An Agency attorney was present at the meeting with the county executive.

A planning council subcommittee had been named to make recommendations on roads near the proposed Agency site, and talks checked earlier informal information on the parkway and land matters. The Bureau of Public Roads had grading work in Arlington County that could begin when funds were made available, and a transfer of funds through the Department of the Interior was advised. Later passages turn to Route 123 from Vienna to Langley Fork, a primary road in the state system, and coming hearings on primary road allocations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020001-0:
Paper on the organization and function of the Office of the Legislative Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency is shown here in part. It sets out how relations with Congress are handled and what laws the Agency sought. One passage notes support from members of Congress for operational activities, including help in having defectors testify before Senate and House committees.

A legislative program for the 84th Congress is listed. Items include medical benefits for dependents abroad, death gratuities, and an allowance toward schooling costs for dependent children overseas. They also include easier retirement rules, home leave on the Foreign Service model, and permanent missing persons legislation. Pay rises for the Director, the Deputy Director, and perhaps six senior officials are also mentioned. A later section places the liaison function in the Office of the General Counsel for administrative purposes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070033-0:
Journal of the Office of Legislative Counsel for 9 March 1956, a Friday, is a short daily log of two numbered items. The first points to a separate memorandum for the files on congressional contacts made by the Director that day, which is not reproduced in the journal itself.

The second records a meeting with Colonel White and division chiefs. The meeting took up how to answer outside inquiries about whether, and in what manner, the Agency handles bids for contract work on translation of unclassified matter. All such inquiries were to go to the Chief, Procurement Division, at 2430 E Street, Northwest. It would reply that the Agency was satisfied with present arrangements with another company and saw no immediate prospect of added contracts. Earlier entries from December 1955, printed below, trace the same question from a congressional office on behalf of a constituent seeking translation contracts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070114-0:
House Document number 159, 83rd Congress, first session, prints a message from the President dated 1 June 1953 transmitting Reorganization Plan number 9 of 1953, sent to the Committee on Government Operations. The plan, prepared under the Reorganization Act of 1949, provides reorganizations in the Council of Economic Advisers in the Executive Office of the President.

The message argues that the Employment Act of 1946 shows a congressional aim to help develop a strong economy, needed to preserve peace, build defenses, raise living standards, and aid trade. A strong economy is described as free, stable, and expanding. The plan shifts work to the Chairman, including employing staff and specialists. It also transfers to the Chairman the function of reporting to the President on the Council's activities, for a clearer and more direct relation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160033-0:
Memorandum on the Commission on Government Security attaches a copy of a Senate joint resolution establishing such a commission, as reported in the Senate, with a Senate report. Members would be appointed by the President, two from the executive branch and two from private life. The Vice President and the Speaker would each appoint four, half from private life. They would study the whole government security program.

The Director of Security had advised in March 1955 that section 8 be retained as a basis for exempting the Agency where security considerations require it. The resolution as passed by the Senate kept that section and somewhat strengthened it, so the Agency appeared adequately protected. H.J. Res. 157, nearly identical, had passed the House with the same section, and the two measures would go to conference to iron out minor differences.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100230008-0:
Printed bill, without a bill number in the portion shown, is titled to facilitate the procurement of doctors and dentists for the Armed Forces. It would do so by providing grants and scholarships for education in medicine and dentistry. A supplementary training and procurement program is set out to meet the needs of the Armed Forces.

Section 1 authorises the Secretaries of the Army, the Navy, and the Air Force to establish annual scholarships for the education and training of doctors and dentists. Section 2 sets up, under the Department of Defense, an Army, a Naval, and an Air Force Medical Services Scholarship Group. Membership is limited to citizens of the United States selected as scholarship beneficiaries who appear fit. A beneficiary must agree that, on completing training, he will accept appointment, if tendered, as a reserve officer and remain an officer until the eighth anniversary of his appointment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200010001-0:
Pages from the Congressional Record, House, for 1956 list communications laid before the House, numbered in sequence and each sent to a committee. Item 1239 is a letter from the national commandant of the Marine Corps League sending its report of activities and newly elected officers for 1956 from its convention in St. Louis, sent to the Judiciary Committee.

Item 1240 sends a report of the Alexander Hamilton Bicentennial Commission dated 12 September 1955. Items 1241 to 1244 send reports of claims paid. One is by the Veterans Administration for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1955 under the Federal Tort Claims Act. Others are by the Canal Zone Government for the year to 30 June 1955 and by the General Services Administration for fiscal 1955. Later items include a Selective Service report to 30 June 1955 and a Navy report on officers above stated ranks by rank and age.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020037-0:
Second copy in the file of S.J. Res. 96 in its reported form, Calendar number 601, Report number 602, introduced 30 June 1953 and reported with amendments on 18 July 1953. The face of the print carries the same recitals on the overseas information program, the presidential message of February 1953, and the June 1953 subcommittee finding on television networks.

Details visible in this copy include the commission's senior staff pay. A Secretary General and an Assistant Secretary General are named, the assistant at not over twelve thousand five hundred dollars a year. Other personnel serve under the Classification Act of 1949 or are obtained from government agencies on a reimbursable basis. Experts and consultants for temporary service are capped at seventy five dollars per day for each individual, and travel and subsistence reimbursement is provided for in the closing sections.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200030036-0:
List of Representatives arranges House members alphabetically by surname, with state, in a table pairing each name with a contact column and a remarks column. Early entries run from Adair of Indiana, Anderson of Minnesota, and Angell of Oregon through Bates and Battle of Alabama. They continue through Boggs of Louisiana, the Boltons of Ohio, Burleson of Texas, and Celler of New York.

Remarks record the degree of acquaintance of an unnamed contact with each member, in plain phrases. The phrases include speaking acquaintance, knew in connection with work on the Department of Agriculture budget, and friendly acquaintance. Others are met casually, fraternity brother, classmate and fairly close friend, quite well, very good friend in OSS days, old friend, and intimate friend. Later pages continue through Curtis, Dodd of Connecticut, Durham of North Carolina, Engle of California, Javits of New York, Judd of Minnesota, McCormack of Massachusetts, and others.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200050016-0:
Briefing memorandum for the Deputy Director, dated 10 January, prepares him for a luncheon with the Texas congressional delegation on 12 January 1955. Attention is called to biographic data at page 137 of the February 1954 Congressional Directory, and changes since that edition are listed.

J. Frank Wilson of the 5th District, Dallas, did not seek reelection, and his seat was won by Bruce Alger, believed to be only the fifth Republican elected to Congress from Texas. Wingate Lucas was succeeded by Jim Wright, John Lyle Jr. by John J. Bell, and Lloyd Bentsen Jr. by Joseph M. Kilgore, whose schooling, Texas legislative service, and Air Force record, including raids in North Africa and the second American air raid on Naples, are set out. A later note states Speaker Rayburn had never received a briefing on Agency activities and was not believed to desire one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200060015-0:
Memorandum for the Director dated 29 December 1955, subject Congressional Contacts, lays out plans to contact key members early in the coming session. Staff would handle routine contacts, but certain members the Director should see himself, to hear their observations and lay before leaders the legislative problems affecting the Agency.

A priority list follows for approval, on the past pattern of weekly Monday luncheons. Senator Russell had accepted an invitation and would debrief himself to Agency people. Representatives of G-2 and the Air Force had asked to sit in, with lunch on Monday 9 January proposed. Senator Saltonstall had returned from a world tour. A later priority names Congressman Zablocki, leader of a recent world trip delegation, for an early lunch and debriefing. A closing note says Congressman Vinson should be kept posted on the new building and new legislation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200090058-0:
Department of State instruction CA-5284, dated 11 February 1955, marked official use only, concerns CODEL Smith, the trip of Senator Margaret Chase Smith of Maine. Addressee posts span Belgrade, Ankara, Athens, Bangkok, Beirut, Bonn, Cairo, Geneva, Hong Kong, London, Paris, Rome, Tokyo, Vienna, and more.

Earlier instructions had announced that the Senator planned to travel around the world the past fall. The aim was to record interviews and impressions for later use on the CBS television program See It Now. The itinerary was split into two trips because of the special Senate session in November, and she completed the European portion and cancelled the rest. She now planned to depart the United States for Tokyo on 16 February on a trip through the Far East, South Asia, the Near East, and Europe. Posts are told to give no notice to the local press of her arrivals or departures unless arranged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200140034-0:
Testimony of Monsignor Bela Varga, taken 26 October 1956 at 4:00 p.m. in the office of the Hungarian National Council in New York City, is printed from the record of the Internal Security Subcommittee. Present were Robert Morris, chief counsel, and Nelson Frank, staff consultant, and the record notes the witness had appeared before and been sworn.

Morris states the subcommittee had for a year inquired into Hungarian Communists in the United States, including representatives to the United Nations and legation staff. In view of the extraordinary developments then taking place in Hungary, it wanted testimony on events there, for its bearing on Hungarian Communists in this country. Asked whether he was an official of the Hungarian postwar government, the witness begins his answer in the portion shown. A later exchange compares events in Hungary with those in Poland.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010004-0:
Pages from the Congressional Record, Senate, for 1956, at page 9501, print material laid before the Senate. They open with resolutions of the California Federation of Post Office Clerks, in convention at Fresno 24 to 27 May. The federation protests questionnaires issued by postmasters in different regional areas to employees concerning outside activities.

The resolutions call the questionnaires an invasion of rights. They note that postal staff are paid for an eight hour day and the rest of the time should be their own if they violate no law. They trace the authority to a St. Paul court decision. The federation mandates its national officers to seek a remedy by legislation or by appeal to a higher court, carried as high as possible. Later pages turn to education beyond the high school and a presidential committee on that subject.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100130001-0:
Hearings volume titled Wiretapping for National Security, before Subcommittee number 3 of the Committee on the Judiciary, House of Representatives, 83rd Congress, first session, Serial number 7. Four bills are listed: H.R. 408, to regulate interception of communications for national security and safety of life; H.R. 477 and H.R. 3552, to authorise interception of communications; and H.R. 5149, on use in court of information intercepted in national security investigations.

Hearing dates are 4 May, 20 May, and 8 July 1953, and the committee membership is printed, under Chairman Chauncey W. Reed of Illinois. Testimony shown turns on section 605 and two readings of intercept and divulge: one, that mere interception is not barred absent later divulgence, and another, that intentional interception itself is covered. The volume runs to hundreds of pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100210002-0:
House report of 30 January 1956, from the Committee on Armed Services, submits a report by Mr. Vinson to accompany H.R. 8710, a bill to amend the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947. The committee reports the bill favorably with an amendment and recommends passage as amended; the amendment strikes 62 Stat. 22 and inserts 69 Stat. 547 at a stated place.

A legislative history recalls that in the 80th Congress the committee consolidated all laws on military procurement into the act approved 19 February 1948. The aim was to re-establish the advertised competitive method for most Army and Navy contracts. Later discussion takes up negotiation without advertising in a declared national emergency, and a Comptroller General view tied to the proclamation of 16 December 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670048-0:
Congressional Record, Senate, pages from 1956 carry House messages at the head of the portion shown. One announces a conference report on the bill for the relief of the city of Elkins, West Virginia; another, that the House insisted on its amendment to S. 3903, on the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, and agreed to a conference, naming its managers.

Further messages cover the bill abolishing the Verendrye National Monument, North Dakota, and House passage of H.R. 5435 on Federal Civil Defense Act procurement. Deeper pages print Civil Service Commission matter: keep the rule that not more than two commissioners share one political party, all appointed by the President with Senate consent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670057-0:
Congressional Record, volume 102, second session, opens a Senate day on Monday 9 April 1956 with the Chaplain's prayer, in the afterglow of Easter. A run of private and general bills follows. Acts listed include S. 101, S. 117, and S. 213, granting permanent residence in the United States to certain aliens, and S. 346, to aid admission of certain aliens.

A middle speech turns to secrecy in intelligence work. A product would be lost if it were known the United States possessed it, so secrecy is necessary. But an essential degree of secrecy differs deeply from secrecy for its own sake. Once secrecy becomes untouchable it invites abuse. If secrecy for its own sake is accepted there is no way of knowing whether the country has a very fine intelligence service or not.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690019-0:
Overseas Allowances Bill is a summary of changes from the original draft submitted for agency clearance on 10 December 1954. Section 111(7) broadens the definition of employee to civilians in government service as defined in presidential regulations, so groups in doubt can be named. A new section 123 lets the President extend the act to the Panama Canal Zone if its separate authority ends.

Section 124 is revised to match the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. A proviso in section 211(1) allows temporary lodging allowance before departure only when lodging costs are in fact incurred. Section 211(3) is changed to a payment or reimbursement authority to limit abuse. Weight limits would cap government liability for storage and transport. A new section for the Administrative Expenses Act of 1946 would give agencies without Foreign Service Act authority a like power, and section 251 is then discussed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690028-0:
Unintroduced print of the Overseas Allowances Act of 1955, in the same form as the bill text in the file. It would consolidate and revise the laws on added compensation for civilian federal employees stationed outside the continental United States and in Alaska. The aims are to ease recruitment, cut turnover, and pay for extra costs and hardships of overseas assignments.

Section 101 declares objectives: codify the compensating provisions into one act. It would give uniform treatment to staff of all agencies so far as conditions of employment justify. It would also provide a basis for more efficient and fair administration, and aid recruitment and retention. Title I then gives definitions and general provisions, and later titles set the allowances. Travel grants in the middle let an employee with over five years in foreign areas claim travel costs of moving his minor dependents to and from the nearest port of entry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200030001-0:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel comments on S. 1094, a bill to amend section 402 of the Federal Employees Uniform Allowance Act. The bill would remove the limitation in Public Law 763 of the 83rd Congress. That limitation required an employee to have been required by law or regulation in effect on 1 September 1951 to wear a uniform.

The memorandum calls the change a desirable liberalization and recommends that the Agency support the proposal. An enclosed explanation states the need more fully: the act should reach employees in occupations where wearing uniforms is deemed necessary and desirable. Since Congress had not yet made appropriations available for paying the benefits, prompt amendment would avoid inequities among uniformed employees when payments begin. The notice of pending legislation form, dated February 1955, and supporting letters are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200120001-0:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated 24 April 1956, comments on S. 3287, a bill to authorize the training of federal employees at public or private facilities, and for other purposes. The bill would let agency heads obtain related training for their employees in other agencies or in non-federal facilities.

From the standpoint of the federal career service as a whole, the memorandum calls the bill a desirable step toward raising employee standards and capabilities. For the Agency, no formal position is needed: it is exempt by reference in section 2(a) of the bill. It holds its own training authority in Public Law 110 of the 81st Congress. No further activity by the Legislative Counsel's office is recommended. The notice of pending legislation, dated 5 March 1956 and sent to the Directors of Training and Personnel, is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200490001-0:
A short CIA legislative file, dated 27 June 1955, circulates H.R. 6591 for comment. Mr. Alger of Texas introduced the bill. It would make all Defense personnel pay ocean shipping charges for their own cars. The charges arise on moves to or from overseas posts. Favourable congressional action is marked as not predicted.

The Director of Logistics explains the bill's origin. It grew out of the Hoover Committee report on government transport. That report urged that military personnel pay such ocean freight themselves. If passed, the change would in practice hit military staff only. Defense civilians already paid those charges. The file holds the routing forms and the opening of the printed bill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100010034-0: A short attachment lists charts made for a proposed Position Schedule bond. The bond would cover CIA staff who handle funds. Eight items are named. Some charts sort bonded staff by place: Washington, United States field posts, or foreign field posts. Others split staff by the Fiscal Division, the Finance Division, or both. A note on the duties of bonded staff is listed too. So is a list of office sites, not for the bonding company. The chart pages are tables whose figures do not read clearly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100040040-0:
An excerpt from Title 18 of the United States Code, kept in CIA legal files, prints federal criminal provisions on threats, extortion, and related offences. One section bars using relief or employment benefits to pressure anyone over race, creed, or political activity, with a fine of up to $1,000 or a year in prison. Other sections cover demanding money by threat and extortion through interstate commerce.

The printed text sets out penalties in detail. Sending a threat to kidnap or injure a person through interstate commerce draws a fine of up to $5,000 or twenty years; other threat communications carry smaller penalties. Part of the scan is garbled, and later pages turn to the handling of foreign mail, but the core of the excerpt is the extortion and threats code.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100090009-0:
A CIA legal memorandum of 15 November 1955 reviews the problem of getting United States passports for aliens. The question first reached the office in 1948, and a legal basis was worked out for granting passports to aliens who had sworn an oath of allegiance to the United States. The Assistant Solicitor General and the State Department's Legal Advisor informally accepted that position, but the head of the Passport Division would not agree, and Agency action stopped in June 1951.

The memo parses the statute, which allows passports only for persons owing allegiance to the United States, and defines citizen, national, and alien. It argues that where the national interest requires it, passport protection can extend to aliens abroad who took an affirmative oath of allegiance, that allegiance being in effect permanent. The Passport Division answered by citing repeal of an earlier law that expressly covered declarants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210032-0:
A CIA legal memorandum for the Director of Security studies the Crypto Security Law. It asks how the law applies to the Agency's own practices. The law guards classified facts about codes, ciphers, and cryptographic systems. It also guards devices built for cryptographic or communications intelligence work. It covers intelligence activity itself. And it covers material gained by reading foreign government messages.

The memo works through the law's definitions. It defines classified information, code and cipher, and communication intelligence. It also defines who counts as an unauthorised person. It then compares this law with the older espionage sections 793 and 794. Those sections turn on intent to injure the United States. This law turns on knowingly and wilfully passing the guarded facts. The memo judges it the stronger shield in its field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030004-0:
A CIA memorandum of 5 February reports a meeting with State Department officers. It went to the Legislative Counsel. Parts of the scan are garbled. The meeting opened the drafting of a revised bill amending the CIA Act of 1949. The State officers raised no objection in principle. They offered technical suggestions on separate parts of the draft.

The memo then works through the bill section by section. One change deletes references to territories and possessions. Another drops a repeated phrase. Others align the travel and allowance sections with Public Law 110. The memo also records the Bureau of the Budget's general position. The Bureau approved foreign travel without changes. But it wanted the staff who would use the provisions briefed on Agency needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030112-0:
A bill draft of 9 June 1947 would establish a Central Intelligence Agency. It opens with findings and a declaration of policy. Congress intends a full and continuous program for national intelligence. A permanent, centralised agency would use all government sources and facilities to the full. It would end wasteful duplication and overlap.

The declared policy backs that design. It would strengthen the government's hand in forming national policy. It would also strengthen its conduct of foreign relations. The common defence and security stay paramount. The bill then turns to the National Security Council. It gives the Council its duties under section 101 of the National Security Act of 1947. It adds direction of the new Agency. The Council would set the Agency's policies and objectives. It would supervise its planning and its coordination of foreign intelligence work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030121-0:
A bill draft would establish a Central Intelligence Agency. Its findings rest on two world wars and the years between. Separate departments gathered foreign intelligence alone. That could not keep the American people, or their elected representatives, properly informed. Events, trends, and plans abroad went unseen. Gathering and analysis must therefore be centralised. All sources should be used to their fullest.

Four programs carry out the Act's purpose. They cover coordination of existing procurement, and research and analysis. They cover dissemination to proper officers and departments. They also cover an administration program to secure all available foreign intelligence. Section 2 then establishes a National Intelligence Authority. A safeguard appears in the text. The departments keep their own authority to collect and disseminate intelligence. The Agency may relieve them of it only under the Act. The Agency gets no police or subpoena powers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200050002-0:
An excerpt from the Code of Virginia prints rules for attorneys at law. It comes from Title 54, on professions and occupations, Article 1. A licence is required to practise. An attorney licensed in another state may still appear in a Virginia case, if he is associated with it. The District of Columbia counts as well. He must prove his standing to the court. He must also swear to execute his office to the best of his ability.

The article then sets penalties and duties. Practising law without authority is a misdemeanour. A clerk, sheriff, or sergeant who acts as attorney in a case touching his own office forfeits one hundred dollars. An attorney is liable to his client for damage caused by neglect. He also faces penalties for taking a client's money and failing to pay it over. Later sections govern admission to the bar.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220002-0:
A CIA memorandum of 25 June 1956 summarises the Supreme Court decision in Cole v. Young. The Court ruled on 11 June 1956. In effect, the Court held that Executive Order 10450 went too far. So far as it lets an agency dismiss a man on loyalty grounds, whatever his post, it passes the power granted by the Act of 26 August 1950. The agency head must judge what the man's retention would mean for national security.

Cole was a food and drug inspector in the Department of Health, Education and Welfare. His post was not sensitive. The charges cited close ties with people reported to be Communists. They also cited support for an allegedly subversive group. The Secretary found his retention not clearly consistent with national security and fired him. The Civil Service Commission refused his appeal, and lower courts ruled for the government. The Supreme Court reversed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220039-0:
A CIA legal memorandum of 27 January gives an opinion on the control of personnel security files. It went to the Director of Security. The year is garbled in the scan. The Director of Security believed a White House memorandum of 13 March 1948 was still in force. That memorandum was quoted in a proposed regulation. It directed that files on the loyalty program be kept in strict confidence. Any subpoena or outside demand for them was to be declined, with referral to the President.

The opinion holds that the directive still stands. Executive Order 9835 has been replaced by Executive Order 10450, but the memorandum survives. The writer checked with Mr. Pollock of the State Department. Pollock advises departments on the Order. He confirmed the memorandum is still in effect. Some changes are planned, but none will come soon. So the regulation should stay in its present form for now.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300230001-0:
A CIA legal memo comments on a draft secrecy agreement, paragraph by paragraph. Names are redacted. The writer takes up comments made on paragraphs 3, 4, 6, and 8. One point concerns grievances. Paragraph 3 bars release of secret facts. Paragraph 6, the writer argues, must mean something more. Read together, carrying even unclassified grievances outside the Agency would be barred by paragraph 6. The two paragraphs are hard to read together.

Another comment claimed paragraph 8 negates paragraph 3. The writer rejects that, since the provisions are separate and additional. The memo ends on whether the agreements can be enforced. Few, the writer doubts, have seriously thought a court could enforce them. Suit would cause the very harm the agreements seek to prevent. A joint Inspector General and General Counsel plan looks more effective for grievances, if not for legal actions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240055-0:
A confidential inventory lists wartime broadcast intelligence documents, one by one. Each entry gives a document's heading, date, and subject. Many come from the Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service of the Federal Communications Commission. One is a daily report on Japan for 10 May 1945. It covers reactions to the unconditional surrender statement. It also covers a protest note on the sinking of the Awa Maru.

Other entries describe intercepts from Chungking and Tokyo. One, dated 25 November 1943, reports damage in Changteh by Japanese soldiers. A handwritten note asks whether Changteh was a Chinese Stalingrad. Further entries cover a Bombay explosion broadcast of 19 April 1944. They cover FCC military intelligence summaries from radio sources. Several pages deal with personalities in Europe and the Far East. Red pencil marks and dates from 1943 and 1944 appear throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300270016-0:
A small CIA file of October 1951 concerns damage to a second family's household effects. Names are redacted. An adjuster's letter reports an investigation. The crating was done in accordance with the Agency's requirements. The damage, the letter says, plainly occurred in transit. It suggests the claim be filed against the carrier. The claim carries the number PO/PCD-1037.

The owner's own statement describes the damage. Almost all items arrived partly damaged. Objects were placed inside containers with no padding, harming contents and containers alike. A framed map of the world, five feet by ten, was packed in its own box. Nails were driven through the map and its frame, ruining both. A Servel Electrolux refrigerator arrived with its top, sides, and front smashed. Its door was sprung so badly that a hand could reach inside. A birch dining chair was cut in about six places.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300290041-0:
A CIA legal memo reviews an opinion on paying for transport of household goods. It went to the Deputy Director (Administration). The earlier opinion is dated 19 August, and the request for review 2 November. The man concerned, whose name is redacted, had returned to Washington from overseas duty. His effects were shipped from New Hampshire to Washington. They had first gone there at Agency expense, for storage during his tour.

The first opinion held against payment. Storage space being tight in Washington was not enough, on its own, to justify the cost under the travel rules. New facts now make the case more complex. The man was detailed to the Agency from the Air Force in August 1951 and assigned to the Far East Division. On 25 February 1952 he was ordered overseas. His orders did not authorise his family to travel with him. The memo works through the Joint Travel Regulations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100010008-0:
A CIA progress report of 28 December 1955 covers war planning by the Office of Training. It went to the Deputy Director (Support). The period runs from 1 July to 15 December 1955. Place names are redacted. The Director of Training has designated a redacted site as the OTR Emergency Relocation Center. The plan relocates the Director, the Administrative Officer, and a secretary to the Agency Relocation Center. About twenty senior personnel go to the training site.

Both cadres have been instructed in their duties and given civil defence credentials. Housing at the site can take 150 more people. Doubt over using the site raises a question: should a new rendezvous point be named, or should OTR get more billets at the Agency centre? A fireproof vault is reserved for vital materials. Material in storage fills three safes. Later pages review country plans, and find their wartime training provisions weaker than the M-day requirements.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100030033-0:
A CIA memo of 13 December 1955 gives OTR comments on country appendices to the operations programs for fiscal 1957 and 1958. Country names are redacted. With one exception, each appendix states that current support will be adequate. No major change in level or character is needed beyond Annex B of the General Plan for fiscal 1958. One appendix adds training for 20 persons, set for the fall of 1957 and spring of 1958.

The programs project little change in past operational patterns. OTR therefore concurs that no major change in training support is needed. Two cautions follow. Deep-cover training requests must reach OTR at least two months ahead. Any major rise in that training will need more instructors in the section.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100140004-0:
A CIA paper describes a Foreign Language Lecture Program. Its purpose is to let interested personnel hear talks in a foreign language. The talks cover the history, institutions, and culture of the area where that language is spoken. Each series runs eight to fourteen lectures. Lecturers must have native fluency. Discussion is normally held in the foreign language. Questions and remarks in English are permitted.

Lectures are planned in Russian, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. Other languages will be added where interest suffices. The activity is open to all. Participants need at least moderate spoken fluency. They attend all lectures and receive formal credit in their training records. Auditors may choose single lectures. Registration runs through the Registrar, OTR, on Form No. 73. Attached topic lists range widely, from nineteenth-century French theatre and novels to art, criticism, and letters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100010013-0:
A CIA draft rule sets policy on acquiring and using office machines and equipment. The scan is heavily garbled, but the main rules can be read. Each office head must ensure full use of existing equipment. Requests for more machines must be tied to the office's improvement program. Central punched card, copying, and recording facilities have been set up inside CIA.

Such facilities serve all components where feasible. No new machines shall be bought while existing facilities are adequate. Separate installations may be kept only where economy, security, or other valid grounds justify them. Special machines are bought only when standard items cannot do the work. The supervisors of the punched card shop figure in the approval chain. The draft closes with duties for approving requisitions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030020-0:
A CIA paper answers a set question: if a ten percent reduction were called for, what would the DDP do? The answer runs in steps. The DDP would first establish his right to set the size of his headquarters organization and overseas stations. He would then cut functions judged duplicatory or unnecessary. An ad hoc group would have six weeks to develop reduction figures. Component chiefs would then have twelve weeks to choose the positions to eliminate.

The rest of the year, 34 weeks, would go to selecting individuals for release. The paper urges a procedure that keeps the most qualified people. It argues against standard Civil Service reduction-in-force principles. Later pages estimate savings of 20 personnel from one program change. Three project activities, the paper suggests, might be run by the armed services instead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000200050009-0:
Instructions explain how to complete the CSB Data Form. The form is to be typed or filled in ink. Item by item, the sheet defines each entry. The subject is the individual's true name, prefaced by Mr., Miss, or Mrs. Present station means the specific assignment. Position title uses codes such as CT(R) or CT(C). Dependents are listed with relationship and age.

Education beyond high school is recorded by dates, school, degree, and major. Employment history runs chronologically from high school, including military service. Kubark employment must show each PCS assignment. A sample form follows, dated 5 January 1954. Its subject is age 30, grade GS-8 since 6 February 1953. The sample shows a wife aged 29, a son of 5, and a daughter of 2. Schooling lists Nebraska University and a U.S. Signal Corps crypto course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100350003-0:
A diary records Operation Alert 1957 at the CIA Relocation Center. Tab A covers 15 July 1957. DD/I personnel assembled at 1100 hours for a briefing on administrative aspects of their stay. At 1300 hours the whole CIA contingent heard the senior war planners of the three Deputy Directors. The Center's commanding officer welcomed the group. The Center must stay ready to care for 650 persons at all times. It also runs a Records Center, a Vital Materials Center, and a Communications Training Center.

The emergency planning officer described the CIA emergency plan. The present concept rests on a force of 602 people. A broader plan would make all surviving Agency personnel members of the emergency team. Expansion to 1,500 or 2,000 persons is under study. Support planning, another speaker said, turns on men, money, materiel, and services.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410015-0:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 April 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. Yugoslavia's administrative divisions for 1956 are complete for March. Albania divisions and Ural-Volga sketch maps follow. Hungary entries cover aluminum plants and nonmetallic minerals. USSR entries include anti-friction bearing plants and mainline locomotive and car plants. Party and government charts for Poland and Yugoslavia appear in revision.

Bulgaria coverage is heavy. Soils maps, smelters, mineral mines, crop regions, and industry by product are all listed. Moscow and Leningrad sheets locate chemical sciences. A Magadan Oblast terrain sheet appears. Later sections cover the Middle East and Africa. Nigeria entries serve the NIS program: mineral deposits, vegetation zones, and mining company property on the Jos Plateau.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100460010-0:
A list of NIS areas was approved by the NIS Committee on 12 July 1955. The list is dated 15 July 1955. Each entry gives an NIS number, a title, and the general area covered. Offshore island possessions are normally included in the related area. Early entries run through Europe. Ireland is NIS 2, France NIS 3, and the Netherlands NIS 4. Denmark includes the Faeroe Islands.

Portugal includes the Azores, Madeira, and the Cape Verde Islands. Spain includes the Canary Islands and Andorra. The USSR entry, NIS 26, covers the state within its de facto boundaries. It includes the Baltic States, northern East Prussia, and Tannu Tuva. Later entries run through Africa. The Belgian Congo includes Ruanda-Urundi. South Africa's entry sweeps in South-West Africa and the protectorates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490008-0:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 242 of April 1957. The Air Force member reported on Subsection 64D, Aircraft Production. State's proposal of 4 March 1957 was acceptable to the Air Force, with one clarification. State would support the economic requirements in full, short of writing a formal contribution. The committee then approved the amended guide.

The Army member presented guides for Section 22 and Supplement II, Coasts and Landing Beaches. Minor nonsubstantive changes were proposed. They had been coordinated with the Navy but not yet with OBI. The committee approved the guides of 22 March 1957 with those changes, subject to OBI review. OBI approved them on 22 April 1957. Other items take up an Air Force proposal for addenda to Chapters I, IX, and VIII.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490017-0:
The NIS Committee held its 251st meeting on 3 September 1957. 251 of 3 September 1957. Personnel changes lead. Lieutenant Colonel Hamilton Avery became the Air Force senior representative effective 21 August 1957. Charles Berney became the alternate. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 5, Belgium. The draft was approved with minor changes. All members praised the chapter's excellence.

This chapter was controlled. Section 12's source comments carried controls, Sections 17 and 18 were controlled in full, and Section 19 was NOFORN. Hong Kong and Macao came next.
