State proposed treating them apart from Nationalist China but binding them in the same chapter. The committee approved. A USSR chapter question follows: whether to split coverage into the USSR as a whole, European USSR, and Asiatic USSR.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100009-0:
A monthly report covers the Cartography Division for August 1957. The division accepted requests for 86 maps and charts. Seventy-four were for CIA and 12 for the Department of State. It completed 97 maps and charts, nine of them for State. Sixty percent of completions concerned the USSR and Satellites. Twenty percent covered the Far East and Western Hemisphere.

Two projects stand out. Maps of Europe and the Arctic were finished on a crash basis for Mr. Stassen at the London Disarmament Conference. A geographic memorandum on the Algerian oil situation was also completed. The NIS Map Coordinator received 13 color proofing jobs and 29 final maps. Ninety-five final maps remained in reproduction. A list of maps completed in August, by requesting agency, follows.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100018-0:
A monthly report covers the Cartography Division for October 1957. The division accepted requests for 78 maps and charts. Seventy-three were for CIA, four for State, and one for the Air Force. It completed 63 maps and charts. Nineteen percent of completions concerned the USSR and Satellites. Sixty-two items remained in reproduction at month's end.

Three projects stand out. A series of 12 maps covers Latin American petroleum for D/GG. A Middle East petroleum map was made for the National Security Council. A special azimuthal map served D/GP. The NIS Map Coordinator received 20 color proofing jobs and 61 final maps in September. One hundred twenty-two final NIS maps remained in reproduction. Tours for outside groups and a list of maps entered in October follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100027-0:
A set of branch comments, headed Recommendations and Problems, comes from monthly reports for July 1957. The Cartography Division's Far East Compilation Branch opens on map names. BGN and NIS policy is the standard for names on D/GC maps. The branch wants freedom to use native forms first, with conventional names in parentheses. BGN gives both forms and leaves the choice to the user.

Work pressure is the second theme. The Terrain unit's load pushes compilation work into the background. A Sinkiang map, companion to a Tibet project, fills an important intelligence gap. It should not be set aside indefinitely for Chapter I work, the branch argues. The Development and Construction Branch reports its reorganization done with few problems. Later comments weigh support duties for the DD/P and other services.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100010003-0:
A CIA form letter sets the terms of an overseas employment agreement. Its imprint is Form No. 51-104, dated June 1948. The letter notifies the employee that the government, represented by CIA, has accepted his employment. Blanks stand for the position and base salary. The employee receives annual and sick leave, retirement coverage, and other benefits under Agency regulations.

Overseas tours normally run 24 months from arrival at post. An employee who ends his assignment early, for reasons within his control, owes money back. Leaving within 12 months makes him liable for all travel expenses. Those cover his own travel, his dependents, household effects, and automobile. Leaving later, but before the tour ends, still leaves him paying return expenses. The letter closes with an acceptance line for the employee's signature.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100030065-0:
A CIA General Counsel memorandum of 23 March 1949 gives an opinion on employing retired Army officers. The Office of Policy Coordination seeks the temporary but extended services of a regular Army officer. He is retired for reasons other than physical disability. The memo works through the dual compensation statutes of Title 5. They are several and somewhat ambiguous, and must be read together.

Section 59a caps combined retired pay and civilian salary at $3,000, with an election allowed. Section 62 bars holding two offices where $2,500 attaches to either. Sections 69 and 70 bar added compensation for one already holding a government post. Those last bars, the memo finds, are no obstacle here. The added service has not been treated as an office. A Comptroller General opinion of 29 December 1948, on a retired naval officer consulting for the AEC, is closely parallel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100140027-0:
A memorandum dated April 27, 1951, from the Public and Governmental Relations Committee of the Technical and Scientific Publishers Group to the Joint Copyright Committee, argues for new legislation on copyright fees. The publishers say the armed services have long refused to pay for large-scale use of copyrighted material, because appropriations law left no funds available for such payments.

Most requests concern technical and scientific works, so the burden falls hardest on those publishers. The memo reviews Section 613 of Public Law 759, which let service funds buy copyrights tied to equipment, but notes that this cover was temporary and unclear. It points to bills S. 966 and H.R. 2821, introduced in February 1951, as the fix, and stresses that military training sections now write their own manuals, making payment for source material more urgent. The copy survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100210029-0:
Addressed to the Deputy Director (Support) on January 13, 1956, a policy memorandum works out how the Agency should set per diem and mileage rates for travel inside the continental United States. The stated problem has three parts: rates must cover necessary travel costs, rest on the circumstances of each trip, and still be applied evenly by every part of the Agency.

The discussion draws on the committee hearings behind Public Law 189, which raised the legal maximum rates on July 28, 1955. Congress, the memo says, acted so that employees would not bear official travel costs themselves. The conclusions reject basing each rate on freshly gathered local cost data for the whole country, calling that plan costly, cumbersome, and unlikely to yield fair rates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100210065-0:
Legal analysis of Public Law 830 of the 81st Congress answers an October 1950 request. It gives an interpretation of parts of the law. The lawyers focus on travel orders. They ask who must direct the travel, and whether the order must be approved in advance. They conclude that expenses such as the shipment of household goods could not be paid. The legal conditions would have to be met beforehand.

A second part deals with contract personnel. Such staff may be required to refund the cost of return travel if they resign before their scheduled tour ends. The Agency may instead choose to treat that cost as an official expense. The Legal Staff argues that one reading of the law pressed on it is wrong. It fails under basic contract principles. The scan is garbled in places, so some details cannot be read with confidence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090007-0:
An Agency analytical paper works through the likely reactions inside the Communist world to the satellite uprisings of the 1950s. It groups the reactions by faction. The first section sketches a Stalinist approach. Die-hard Stalinists, it argues, would blame the revolts in Poland and Hungary. They would also blame the East German rising and the 1953 strikes in Czechoslovakia. The cause, in their view, was the abandonment of Stalin's methods by his successors.

The paper lists the concessions such critics would attack. They include the overtures to Tito. They include the purge of Beria and the trimming of the secret police. They include the 20th Party Congress line that several national roads to Communism are possible. A later section sketches a Leninist approach. It demands a return to Lenin in deeds as well as words. It contrasts today's party bosses and managers with the revolutionaries of Lenin's time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090016-0:
A staff paper for the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence weighs incentive pay for foreign languages. It states its problem plainly. The aim is to summarize the pros and cons of paying staff extra for gaining language and area knowledge. Its facts compare practice elsewhere. One organization, its name removed in review, already grants such pay.

The State Department has no such plan. It instead trains staff at the Foreign Service Institute when assignments require it. The Foreign Operations Administration is in the same position. Arguments against the plan question its premise. Staff may need courses made available, not extra incentive. Several hundred employees had already taken outside courses at their own expense, after working hours. That was in the academic year 1953-54. Poorly planned incentive pay, the paper warns, could also produce disorganized study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100120003-0:
Changes to a table of organization are requested in a memorandum dated February 26, 1957, from the Agency's Director of Training to the Chief of the Management Staff. The request concerns the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. Over the previous four years, the memorandum says, that staff's function and workload had grown and changed in character, creating a need for a different spread of professional skills.

The requested changes, set out in an attached tab, are described as minor next to the adaptations the staff had already made. They include technical support for building new selection and placement testing programs and improving existing ones. One item would reclassify a psychometrist post graded GS-7 into a senior psychology post at GS-13, giving research support to the recruiters' testing program for clerical and professional staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100130002-0:
A memorandum to the Deputy Director (Plans) is sent through the Deputy Director (Support). It outlines what the Agency's Office of Training can still do after a ceiling was placed on personnel strength. The ceiling dates to July 31, 1955. The paper's purpose is to state the office's capability to meet training requirements. It covers the period while the office adjusts to that ceiling.

Enough time had passed, the paper says, to show one thing. Training can in general continue at the current level. But some essential activities were understaffed in July 1955. Positions and people have therefore been reshuffled inside the office. A few programs judged to be of relatively low priority have been cut back. One named example stands out. The Reading Improvement Program staff is being reduced from six people to two.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200020003-0:
A printed program sets out a CIA presentation at the National War College. The audience was the staff, faculty, and student body. The session ran from 1330 to 1630 on September 9, 1957. It was held in the R&S Building on Ohio Drive, Potomac Park. Lt. General Charles Cabell, the Deputy Director, opens with welcome and introduction.

Lyman Kirkpatrick, the Inspector General, follows. He speaks on the origin, missions, and structure of the Agency. After a break, Robert Amory speaks on the Agency, the intelligence community, and the National Security Council. Frank Wisner then covers foreign and counterintelligence operations. Allen Dulles, the Director, closes with psychological and paramilitary operations. Speaker biographies follow. They trace careers that run back through the wartime OSS and the Central Intelligence Group to the Agency of 1957.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200040001-0:
A memorandum for the record dated January 24, 1957, reports on a two-week recruiting effort for Agency junior officer trainees at the major academic institutions in California. It describes the current situation, praises the full-time recruiter, and stresses the huge geographical area he alone must cover. Recruiting methods used by other government agencies and by private enterprise are held up for comparison.

The findings are sobering. Students worry about insecurity in government work and the risk of being cut in a reduction in force. The pay offered to entering trainees does not begin to match private enterprise, and the clandestine life, with little job information given in advance, does not help. Suggestions include a more open approach, earlier contact with students, and better placed consultants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200070008-0:
A schedule and briefing pack for Project Useful No. 3 covers two weeks. The project ran from October 15 to 26, 1956. The pack opens with facts the visiting officers should know. Security comes first. Their presence is not to be known beyond those authorized. If friends at the Pentagon ask, they are to say they are in Washington for conferences. The conferences would be at another Defense Department installation. Even inside the Agency they may not reveal the nature of the meetings.

The attendance lists name senior officers from across the services, with rank and assignment. They include a lieutenant colonel from Headquarters, Strategic Air Command. They include the Director of Intelligence of the Alaskan Air Command. They include a Navy commander from the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, and an Air Force instructor. The program thus brought serving officers inside the Agency for two weeks of closely held sessions.

A draft memorandum signed by Allen W. Dulles, Director of Central Intelligence, initiates a Foreign Language Resources Program. Addressed to the three deputy directors, it sends them a description of the program and the text of an announcement to be distributed to all employees. The Director of Training, it says, will announce the policies, standards, and procedures for the parts of the program in his charge.

The program description starts from need: effective work requires ever greater numbers of staff with foreign language skill. Its machinery includes an inventory of the language resources of staff employees, kept current from proficiency test records and personnel files. The Director of Training would develop and run the tests on which the inventory rests, and the Director of Personnel would maintain the records.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200220010-0:
A review dated January 11, 1956, takes up instruction concerning Communism and related subjects across the Agency. Agreement is reported on one point. The Communism curriculum and the arrangements for handling it need revision. The present courses are called good and well used. Duplication between them should still be cut. Further offerings are needed. The Agency's considerable instructor strength could be used to better effect.

The writer notes a gap. No systematic analysis has ever been made of the full range of Agency needs in this field. The needs cover training on Communism and Communist Party operations. Proposed lines of study follow. They include courses on how Communist action shows itself in particular areas and countries. They include judging party capabilities and likely moves. They include an anti-Communist operations course built largely on the one then offered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300020011-0:
Weekly Activities Report number 46, dated November 20, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. Significant items are again none. The school reports that, after the Director of Training presented the Language Development Program, a survey of language skills and current language study was hastily carried out in the IO Division. Statistics and other information were also supplied to an officer taking up a new assignment.

The Russian Advanced Workshop began on November 18 and would run to March 20, 1959, with enrollment of five in reading, eight in grammar, and eight in speaking. The Slavic department's November 12 meeting was given over to teaching method, with a fifty-minute demonstration of structural drills.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030001-0:
Weekly Activities Report number 43, dated October 30, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It reports arrangements made at the Far East division's request. Five people would receive oral proficiency testing in Thai. The testing would be done at the Foreign Service Institute. The Agency had no one qualified to sit on a Thai testing panel. The division's standing request also came up. It asks for two Japanese-trained junior officer trainees a year.

The report lists books ordered for the school. They include a history of the Reformation and a study of the Greek mind. Hungarian Basic Reading I, begun on October 13, had seven students. They were drawn from both the intelligence and plans directorates. An advanced Russian workshop was announced to start on November 18.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030010-0:
Weekly Activities Report number 34 comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It carries an unusual significant item. The item gives a blunt count of the Agency's own effort against its language problem. Current plans, it says, would give intensive basic training at headquarters in the coming year to few people. Two people would train in Chinese, one in Russian, and three in Persian. For Arabic the figure is none. For anything else, none, except a few in French and German.

A couple of people would get advanced Chinese at Yale. An attached report adds smaller news. It comes from the Deputy Chief for Area Training and is dated August 27, 1958. It notes that attendance in the area course Moscow-Peking Axis had held up very well to date.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300070007-0:
Weekly Activities Report number 37 comes from the Agency's School of International Communism and the USSR. It covers September 12 to 18, 1958. The special course on the USSR being given for OSI was slowly filling. Five further applications had come in through informal channels. One more was expected, bringing the total to eleven. The school had been assured the number would reach fifteen. A class of twelve, though, was judged quite adequate, rather than forcing the point.

The report owns a mistake. An error about this course in the latest training schedule had crept in. The fault lay in its own office. The writer is sure it will not affect the course. A discussion of evaluations follows. In it, a supervisor insists he wants assessments only where he asks for them, which is often.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110002-0:
Weekly Report number 2 comes from the Agency's Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers January 8 to 14, 1958. The chief and the Chief of the Assessment Branch conferred with the head of RI. His key administrative staff joined them. The subject was a plan that would, over time, lead to the assessment of all RI personnel. The purpose of that assessment program would be to help in career planning for the people concerned.

Testing business follows. The chief and the Chief of the Testing Services Branch met the Chief of the Personnel Procurement Branch. They discussed the use of tests in clerical recruiting. A training item notes a limit on one course. Incomplete electronic gear would seriously limit its aims at its first presentation. Enthusiasm to do the best possible job was undampened.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110039-0:
Weekly Report number 40 comes from the Agency's Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers October 1 to 7, 1958. Two meetings that week took up one subject. It was the evaluation program for the integrated JOT program. Both meetings were called at the request of the Chief of the Plans and Policy Staff. Training chiefs and the A&E staff concerned agreed on a format. Each student would get a two-part report.

The first part would cover what the student learned in the course. It would go into the official personnel file. The second part would be marked Eyes Only. It would carry the franker material. Attached guidance lists the kinds of observations instructors should record. It stresses that the list is only suggestive. Any observation judged significant should be written down, whether or not it fits an item on the list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400030070-0:
The Agency's Intelligence School Weekly Report number 6 covers February 7 to 13, 1958. Its significant item is a finish. The first running of Intelligence Research (Techniques) was completed on February 7. A graduation party was attended by the Director of Training, school leadership, faculty, and students. The eight students took the full-time, four-week course. They were warm in their final critiques. Several recommended that analysts take a refresher every three to five years.

Because the students' research experience ran from three months to five years, the course was run as a seminar. That produced a lively exchange. Tentative plans would offer it to OSI again in March. Classroom space in the R&S area, the report adds, continues to be a major problem. The Clerical Training counts for the week are appended.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400090001-0:
Weekly Activity Report number 51 comes from the Agency's Junior Officer Training Program. It covers December 17 to 30, 1958. Briefings are being arranged for the trainees heading into Operations Course number 8. A morning briefing on February 3 would serve the JOTs themselves. An afternoon session the same day would serve the married trainees and their wives. It would probably be held in the R&S Auditorium.

Reports had come in from two sources. They were the instructors in the Survey of International Communism and the seminar leaders in American Heritage. The reports were being analyzed. The report quotes a division chief forwarding reports by former trainees. He praised a triple-threat combination. It joined language training, area training, and publishable reporting. The report also notes one silence. No word had yet come back from the A&E Staff's interviews with trainees who planned to resign.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100002-0:
A report of the Working Group on Trainees is dated March 25, 1952. The group belonged to the Career Service Committee. It followed terms of reference issued the previous October. The group describes the two training efforts it found on the ground. One was a professional training program of limited scope, run by the Office of Training. Exceptionally qualified young men and women were specially selected and employed. After basic training they were assigned on to the offices that would use them.

The other was a highly developed training program serving the covert offices. Where the two efforts collide, the report proposes a referee. The Professional Selection Panel should arbitrate and recommend assignments. A full section weighs the proper size of the trainee program. It takes the Agency's needs, turnover, and eventual steady-state requirements together. Precise figures for any of them were not to be had.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400010010-0:
A memorandum dated September 17, 1954, to the Director of Central Intelligence, sent through the Director of Training, reports on a university-sponsored training project whose names are removed in review. Late in 1952 the writer had outlined an approved project for training Agency personnel in the Arabic language and in the Near and Middle East area. Its aim was academically recognized results for a small, highly qualified group, with arrangements designed for the greatest practical achievement and security at reasonable cost.

Pending final standards, the memorandum sets interim minimums. Anyone whose duties involve working with substantive material on a foreign area must complete an area orientation course of not less than sixty-four hours, at the Agency or at a university. Earlier academic training of comparable quality would count in its place.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400080004-0:
Comments on the Inspector General's survey of the Office of Training go to the Director of Central Intelligence. They travel in a memorandum dated June 4, 1954. The survey had been proposed the previous May. Its aim was an objective view of the office's problems. It would also give advice on improving the training effort. The memorandum works through the Inspector General's recommendations. It takes up the related questions that still required further study and decision. It promises companion papers on some of them.

Its first substantive point is a gap that runs through the whole file. There is no agreed definition of linguistic competence for intelligence personnel. There is no firm Agency policy on language proficiency levels. There is none on the area specialization that operating components should aim at. Those levels are what components use when they set their training requirements.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100210004-0:
A paper dated February 1, 1951, sets out how the Procurement and Supply Office is organized and what it does. Its problem is growth. The office was to provide complete logistical support for all Agency operations. Related planning, transportation, real estate, and construction organizations were being transferred into it. That combination required a pattern of organization with two strengths. It had to supervise far-flung activities. It had to distribute responsibility properly among them.

The functions listed reach two years ahead. Requirements are to be prepared two years in advance, by quarters. Logistical annexes are to be prepared for specific projects. An operations element would coordinate with the operating divisions day by day. It would advise the chief on the capabilities and needs of future operations. It would act as his liaison with the divisions the office served.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220003-0:
A staff paper on the Security Staff of the Agency's Logistics Office argues for making formal what already worked in practice. When the office's present organization was approved in March 1953, one placement was made. The security element was placed inside the Administrative Staff. In fact, the Security Officer had reported directly to the Chief of Logistics. That direct line covered every security matter needing his attention. Security work had been handled successfully through that line. It also ran through direct contact with the office's components.

The proposal would establish the Security Staff as a separate staff. It would report directly to the chief. Its workload data runs to clearances of every kind. They include commercial contractor clearances and continuing liaison clearances. They include contact, covert, and special purpose clearances. Advice, processing, correspondence, and the keeping of files and records are included too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100240029-0:
Comments and recommendations on an Agency Administrative Branch, Tab F-4 of a survey, begin with structure: the branch's organization appears satisfactory. Its proposed table of organization, reflecting combined military and civilian strength, adds one position, a Military Personnel Officer. That is no real addition, since an active duty military man already fills the job. The table should be adequate, though not excessive, a judgment based on experience with like elements carrying like workloads.

The Budget and Fiscal Section draws a sharper finding. The IBM listing of funds does not arrive until the middle of the following month. It can verify an allottee's own records after the fact, but it is practically useless for telling him, before he obligates money, whether funds are available.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100005-0:
Revised mission and functions statements for the Agency's Office of Research and Reports are dated December 1956. They restate the office's work around economic intelligence. A secretariat element is charged with one continuing duty. It gives staff support to the economic intelligence committee structure. It arranges working groups to provide economic support on products of importance to national security. It gives those groups guidance and staff support as they work.

The Coordination Staff carries the production system. It is responsible for coordinating foreign economic intelligence production. It is responsible for the development, implementation, and control of that production. All of it serves the office's responsibilities. Its chief determines what foreign economic intelligence should be produced, for planning purposes. He oversees requirements and evaluation. He convenes ad hoc committees and consultant panels to help carry the research load.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100032-0:
A short set of tables from September 1952 records how analysts in parts of the Office of Research and Reports spent their branch effort. One table lists work types side by side: basic branch projects, special projects, reading, evaluations, requirements, training, export control, an estimates file, administration, consultation, and internal and external contacts. Editing, a China study, lost time for moving, and miscellaneous work also appear.

A second form, for the Organizations Branch, asks each analyst to log time to the nearest quarter hour by category. Categories cover branch projects, background research, outside service, in-box reading and filing, secretarial work, planning, and leave. Together the sheets show how managers tried to measure analytic time, even though many table cells are blank in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100041-0:
A chart lists interdepartmental working groups serving the Economic Defense Advisory Committee structure, with each group's charge stated in brief form. The shared aim was to supply fully processed, evaluated, and timely material to policy and operations staffs. One group dealt with Title II list controls and Battle Act rules, while another studied transit trade, meaning goods bound for the Soviet Bloc through ports and inland depots worldwide.

Other groups covered cargo transport controls, shipping policy, and coal supplies for Western European states that relied on Bloc coal. A Far Western group weighed commodity controls, shipping and transshipment controls, and ways to cut reliance on the East. Each entry cites the paper that set the group's terms, giving a compact guide to early export-control work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200140001-0:
A Management Staff report on Project 3-10 tackles a plain problem: how to build and keep verified records of time Agency staff spent overseas, on permanent or temporary duty. The report follows an April 1958 memo that sent out a questionnaire on overseas duty. Planners needed sound figures to design a better retirement program, and verified service records would later support claims of retirement eligibility.

Work was split into three phases, each open to separate handling. One phase weighed the best way to gather planning data, using a survey of past overseas service by current staff. The report warns that needed records sit in many places, not one central file, and that proving past service across government could cost more time and money than the gain would justify. Options are weighed against that cost.

House Report No. 957, dated 20 August 1959, sends S. 2162 back to the House with a favorable report and an amendment. The bill would set up a health benefits program for government employees. The Committee on Post Office and Civil Service replaced the whole text after the enacting clause with a substitute, printed in italics, and explained the effect of that change in its report.

Agency views form a large part of the volume. A letter from Budget Director Maurice H. Stans sets out where the Bureau of the Budget stood on the bill's administrative terms. A Civil Service Commission letter of 5 August 1959 gives that body's views to Chairman Tom Murray. Readers can follow how the House reshaped a Senate bill and how the executive branch reacted line by line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030012-0:
Roger W. Jones, Chairman of the United States Civil Service Commission, gave a statement on 12 August 1959 to the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. His subject was S. 2162 and matching bills on health insurance for federal staff. He brought two Commission staff members with him, Warren Irons and David Lawton, who had done much of the work on health bills.

Jones praised the committee's close study, saying the hearings had sharpened most major issues. He called the bill a pioneering effort in a hard field and warned against seeking a perfect law. What was needed, he argued, was a flexible bill with firm policy lines. He also stressed broad coverage: a plan must reach the largest number of staff, low-paid staff included, and costs must match coverage.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030021-0:
A Bureau of the Budget letter dated 4 August 1959 answers a House chairman's request of 8 July for views on S. 2162, a bill to provide a health benefits program for government employees. The Bureau writes from the Executive Office of the President in Washington. Its opening history traces Administration support for a voluntary health insurance program for federal staff back to 1956, with plans put forward in several earlier years.

Each plan, the letter notes, tried to improve on the last. In 1958 the Administration gave priority to pay rises and asked that health insurance wait. The letter also lists how federal pay and benefit spending had already grown through pay rates, annuities, premium pay, and retirement changes. Its closing aim is a sound program, with benefit levels in line with private industry plans and a firm base of facts for later growth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030067-0:
Pages from the Congressional Record for the Senate open with the reading and blanket confirmation of 2,702 nominations for the Regular Army, the Marine Corps, and the Navy and Naval Reserve. The presiding officer states the names from the Executive Calendar, and the Senate confirms them en bloc without objection. Senator Johnson of Texas notes that almost 3,000 names were confirmed at once and asks that the President be told at once.

Later pages in the same set turn to the federal health benefits bill. One passage describes an advisory council made up of the two Post Office and Civil Service committee chairmen, four other public officials, and five presidential appointees, one drawn from employee groups. A health benefits fund and the rules on contributions and costs are also set out. The set mixes routine Senate business with bill detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300190015-0:
A memorandum for the record dated 7 January 1959, filed in the Executive Registry, firms up dates for a round of Senate Foreign Relations Committee appearances. William Macomber, Assistant Secretary of State for Congressional Affairs, telephoned the news. The State Department would appear on 14 January, Defense on 16 January, and an economic briefing would follow on 21 January. CIA would appear on 23 January 1959. Macomber stressed that no further invitation should be expected.

The committee treated Senator Green's December letter to the President and the President's reply as notice enough, since the President had asked Secretary Dulles to coordinate the meetings. Later talk in the memo looks ahead to likely questions, drawn from the past year's Taiwan Straits crisis, Middle East events, Berlin, and the revolution in Cuba. It also looks to what the next year might bring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020099-0:
A mission and functions statement defines the Geography Division within the Office of Research and Reports, Geographic Research Area. The division produces geographic material in support of the CIA and, as required, other parts of the intelligence community. Its duties start with planning, recommending, and carrying out regional and systematic research on the geographic character of areas of interest.

Further duties cover special geographic studies for government departments in fields such as evasion and escape, unconventional warfare, targeting, territorial problems, and map appraisal. The division also follows Bloc work in geodesy, gravimetry, and cartography, and reports on trends and events of geographic weight. Branch-level sections repeat these tasks by region, including the Near East and Africa, and include producing the CIA contribution to map and chart appraisal work for the survey program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200220005-0:
A draft of the China satellite memorandum, dated 2 September 1958, survives in rough type. A report that a Soviet embassy first secretary in Mexico said China was preparing, with Soviet help, to launch a satellite opens the case. The Geography Division had been studying missile test range sites in Communist China and found that site needs and geographic factors together pointed to a probable place.

Soviet cooperation, the draft argues, would likely bring Soviet personnel, missiles, launching equipment, and support equipment. A transplanted Sputnik could be expected to fly in the same manner as the three earlier Soviet Sputniks from Tyura Tam. The Inner Mongolia steppes north of Peiping again supply the terrain match. Hazard discussion gives a danger radius around the site and a far larger distance around the booster impact area.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200220014-0:
A Current Intelligence Weekly Summary item dated 13 February 1958 previews the International Conference on the Law of the Sea, opening at Geneva on 24 February under United Nations sponsorship. About eighty-nine countries would send representatives to draw up agreements on many points of maritime law. The hardest problem, the item says, would be the extent of the territorial sea, the belt over which a coastal state holds full sovereignty.

Other subjects listed are methods of measuring territorial waters, innocent passage for ships and its regulation, and coastal state rights in the contiguous zone beyond territorial waters. Fishing rules and conservation of marine resources on the high seas complete the list. One passage treats Indonesia, which claimed all waters around its islands as national waters. It also claimed a twelve nautical mile territorial sea measured from straight baselines joining the outermost island points.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060004-0:
Weekly Activities Report No. 22 from the Chief of Headquarters Training, dated 4 June 1959, covers 27 May through 2 June 1959. One significant item reports a study finished for the Director on a Thursday in late May, with word that a senior official intended to call a meeting on the subject soon. Two staff members, asked about papers for a Latin American project, said they would prepare no formal papers. Their views were already in the basic concept paper and its attachment of typical situations, they said.

Instructor training gets a warm note from an enjoyable session. Later items warn against saying the wrong thing when answering student questions and urge recruiting steady stand-by instructors for the next course. A familiarization course, No. 15, began on Monday, 1 June with eleven students enrolled, though one applicant from a staff office cancelled on the opening day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060022-0:
Weekly Activity Report No. 19 survives as a fragment that opens in mid-discussion, dated by an 8 May meeting inside the text. Staff had met with Clandestine Services personnel over a revised outline and suggestions from a Monday night meeting. One reviewer hinted, delicately, that he detected an FI tint in the newer outline. The writer answers that this could hardly come from long association with that activity. He also notes an added appendix for cold war reporting judged of immediate use.

No further meetings with Clandestine Services staff were planned until a first draft was ready for comment. A second item follows a writer still reviewing material before drafting. He visited the Atomic Energy Commission on 11 May and the Office of Civil and Defense Mobilization on 12 May, finding confusion and few materials there. A field trip passage describes a demonstration with empty bottles used for field explosives.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100010015-0:
H.R. 13740, introduced by Mr. Boyle on 12 August 1958 and sent to the Committee on Ways and Means, would amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Its aim is a credit against individual income tax of thirty percent of amounts paid as tuition or fees to certain public and private colleges and universities. The bill adds a new section, numbered 39, to the part of the code dealing with credits against tax.

The general rule allows the credit to an individual for sums paid for himself or others, as the text goes on to define. A limit passage provides that tuition and fees count only above the total of scholarships and fellowship grants received for the same period. A share of other allowances described in the bill is also excluded. Definitions and limits fill the short printed text, which is a bill as introduced, not a report or an enacted law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100170034-0:
Paper IAC-D-57/91, dated 4 February 1958, gives a post-mortem on National Intelligence Estimate 11-4-57, Main Trends in Soviet Capabilities and Policies, 1957-1962, dated 26 November 1957. As in the estimate before it, most major issues lay in the military field. The chief bone of contention was the present strength and future growth of the Soviet heavy bomber and tanker force. How far new weapon systems would shape its size and mix was also disputed.

Findings open on a positive note. Reporting on the USSR keeps improving as overt information grows, Soviet leaders speak more openly at home, Western contacts widen, and statistical secrecy narrows. Later passages call for a fresh look at cost analysis methods. They also call for better matching of estimated military outlays against Soviet budget and material accounts, noting a habit of judging the burden of defense spending in a narrow way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100220001-0:
A Top Secret signature record and cover sheet heads a long file whose attached paper concerns a Defense Department study on defense against ballistic missiles. The printed form warns that it stays attached to each Top Secret document until the paper is downgraded, destroyed, or sent outside the CIA. Access is limited to control staff and those whose duties touch the matter. Columns are provided for receipt, release, and every person who sees the document.

The attached paper, tied to paper IAC-D-81 and a September committee proposal credited to General Collins, reports an ad hoc committee study prepared at the direction of the Intelligence Advisory Committee. The Board of National Estimates had reviewed the report but did not propose to send any written comment. The file runs to many pages of registry and circulation matter beyond the study note itself.

A clean copy of the budget analysis on overt intelligence collection, dated 1 November 1954, matches the tab version in this band. It asks which joint arrangements, beyond the Council directives, would produce an effective and coordinated overt collection program in 1956. Publications procurement leads: an advisory committee on foreign language publications, with subcommittees for procurement, use, and reference, was building shared methods for foreign language material across member agencies.

Greater Washington support for publications procurement officers at major Foreign Service posts is noted as a gain. Map procurement follows, aimed at foreign maps for the whole community. Later pages describe uniform indexes kept across offices and resident agencies so collection effort is not duplicated, naming Agency offices, Army intelligence, State, and the air technical center. Radio monitoring under a Council directive closes the visible sections, covering foreign propaganda and press broadcasts.

A memorandum from the Office of National Estimates, dated 18 February 1957, estimates the probable effects of United Nations sanctions against Israel backed by the United States. The assumed resolution would hold until Israel complied with the call to withdraw from Sinai and the Gaza Strip. The United States would halt government help, block Israeli funds, and block private transfers of goods and dollars.

Arab states and the USSR, which had already stopped oil shipments to Israel, would strongly support such a program. Most Arab-Asian and many Latin American states would comply. Money figures stress Israel's exposure: forty-five million dollars a year in American help and over one hundred fifty million raised privately in Western countries. The memo judges it almost certain that a sustained program of economic sanctions would in the end compel Israel to yield.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300090022-0:
Minutes numbered IAC-M-350 record a committee meeting at a quarter to eleven on 1 July 1958, with Director Allen W. Dulles presiding and the usual member list for State, the services, the Joint Staff, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Early business concerns material on the Polish situation that was circulated at the meeting itself.

Members agreed that this material should be coordinated and submitted for review as a special estimate at the next regular meeting. A second item takes up priority national intelligence objectives, in annexes to a Director's directive. After discussion, members agreed it was fitting for subsidiary priority objectives to be set below the national level in the manner proposed. The minutes are a sanitized copy, with some matter removed, and record decisions in brief numbered form.

A contract amendment letter dated February 1959, numbered with a 59 series file mark and marked copy of five, goes to the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation at Burbank, California. It refers to a contract entered into on 15 June 1957 between the government and the company. Under the changes clause of the general provisions, the contracting officer's directions made it necessary to amend the scope of work in Appendix I.

Appendix I is therefore deleted in full and the attached Appendix I put in its place, so the scope better matches the parties' intentions. Under a price redetermination part of the schedule, the parties negotiated and agreed final contract prices for Sections A and B of the new appendix, set out in an attached appendix. A later passage adds a sum to a tentative billing price for a further section; the figures there are partly garbled, so no amount is quoted here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200010101-0:
A negotiated contract, rendered in the heading as Contract No. HF-AP-1910, names The Firestone Company, Incorporated, of 3685 Broadway, Buffalo, New York, as contractor. The estimated contract price is given as 25,000 dollars. The contractor agrees to furnish the facilities and deliver all supplies and perform all services set out in the attached schedule, for the consideration stated.

Rights and duties of the parties are governed by the schedule, Appendix I, and the general provisions. Together with the signature page and a certificate, they make up the contract. Where schedule and general provisions clash, the schedule controls. A termination passage in the middle requires the contractor, on termination, to hand over completed work and material. Plans, drawings, data, information, and reports produced or acquired in connection with the work ended by the notice are also handed over.

Secretary means the Secretary, any Assistant Secretary of the department, and the head or any assistant head of the federal agency. His duly authorized representative means any person or board, other than the contracting officer, authorized to act for him. Contracting Officer is likewise defined as the person signing for the government and any properly designated successor.

Subcontracts are defined to include purchase orders under the contract. A patent passage in the middle grants a license to the contractor, with a right to grant sublicenses. The license is assignable to a successor of the part of the contractor's business to which an invention belongs. The same clause sets duties to deliver interim reports on inventions, and consequences if the contractor fails to deliver them on time.

General provisions in this copy cite two regulation sources for their definitions, ASPR 7-103.1 and AFPI 7-403.1. Secretary covers the Secretary, Under Secretary, or any Assistant Secretary, and the head or assistant head of the executive agency. A duly authorized representative is any person or board, other than the contracting officer, cleared to act for the Secretary. Contracting Officer and subcontracts are defined on the same pattern as companion copies.

A royalties passage in the middle requires the contractor to report in writing, in quadruplicate, to the contracting officer as soon as practical after signing. The report states whether any royalties over a stated threshold have been or are to be paid. The threshold figure is partly garbled in the scan. Confidential paper dated 13 May 1958 sets out a plan for an Overseas Career Corps for the Agency. Members would be chosen from the Career Staff who had shown, through actual overseas service, both ability and intent to spend a large part of a career abroad. The plan borrows features from the Foreign Service while aiming for more flexibility.

Selection would run through nomination to a Selection Board, and the Career Council would recommend the size of the Corps each year. Members would be paid from confidential funds, and Intelligence Officers and Support Officers in the Corps would follow Foreign Service Officer pay scales. The paper also covers removal when overseas service or future usefulness fell below standard.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100020017-0:
Draft dated 7 October 1960 lists what the Agency's Management Staff did in the DD/S area. The list runs from 1 April through 30 September 1960. It was drawn up for the Hull Committee report. First comes a depth survey of the Office of Logistics, with a new plan for how that office is run. The plan would put a single supply system under one head. It spans the Procurement, Supply, and Transportation Divisions.

Working level talks then built support for one control point for the whole supply system. The same work set down where the three divisions overlap. Later items cover the Real Estate and Construction Division and the Printing Services Division. They note changes to contract invoices that cut both copies and prep time. The list also backs a new way to fund procurement. It ends with a full review of how upkeep work is run.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100070003-0:
Memo dated 25 January 1954 goes to the Chairman of the Project Review Committee. It puts forward a project to build a lasting Agency Records Center. The cost is put at 405,000 dollars. A full project outline goes with the memo. The outline bears the assent of the Director of Security and the Chief of General Services. The Comptroller and the Chief of Logistics assent as well. The Acting Deputy Director for Administration adds his approval on the way up.

Annex pages size the planned building at about 21,290 square feet. It would hold roughly 40,000 cubic feet of records. That works out near two cubic feet of records for each square foot of usable floor. The new centre would take the place of stopgap stores. It would bring records no longer in daily use into one building made for the task.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100070030-0:
Table set in the Agency's files estimates production of Bison and Bear heavy bombers at named Soviet airframe plants, numbered 1, 18, 22, and 23, under two 46-hour shifts per week. Four estimates are laid out side by side, each giving unit totals by plant for mid-1960 and mid-1962. Combined totals rise across the estimates, reaching into the thousands of aircraft by mid-1962 in the highest case.

Assumptions are printed with the tables. Production acceleration was to begin 1 July 1957 at Plants 23 and 18, and first direct manhours on heavy bomber output fell on the same date at Plants 1 and 22. Later tables work month by month, showing monthly and cumulative output from a production go-ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100110062-0:
Talk text in the Agency's files presents the current picture of naval vessel construction in Communist China, covering types under construction, volume, building facilities, and China's ability to make components. It sets aside the role of the junk. Building modern Soviet-model naval vessels in China had changed the naval balance in the Far East, with submarines, escort vessels, and smaller types already delivered to the fleet.

China lacked the industrial base to run the program alone, so Soviet technical help and material support were extensive, though their scale was not known. Chiang-nan Shipyard had built W-class long range submarines since 1953, and work on that class was believed to have begun at Wuchang Shipyard on the Yangtze as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100160193-0:
Analyst Record of Time Distribution, Form No. 70-7 dated 1 April 1954, is a filled working sheet rather than a report. Columns split an analyst's time by day and project among research and writing, editing and supervising, and consultations and conferences. Conference time is split again among internal ORR, internal Agency outside ORR, and outside the Agency.

Rows at the foot give totals and percentages for staff in several branches, identified by short branch codes, with research time by far the largest share in most rows. A second part lists personnel included in the totals. The sheet shows how ORR managers tracked where analyst hours actually went, project by project, across a working period.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020032-0:
Agency priority requirements sheet dated 27 November, year partly cut in the scan, sets basic requirements on Hungarian water transportation. Ocean items come first: merchant fleet statistics by number, type, area of operation, and general traits, plus reporting on single ships by itinerary, size, age, engines, equipment, and condition. Additions to the fleet by building at home or abroad or by purchase are also wanted.

Chartering of Western flag vessels, cargo traffic, and ton-kilometre performance follow. Inland waterway sections then ask for fleet numbers by type, covering self-propelled and dumb barges, cargo ships, tank barges, and tugs, with tonnage, ownership, age, and seasonal patterns of traffic by cargo. Where totals cannot be had, details of known facilities will serve.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020069-0:
Agency memo dated October 1956 asks leave for a visitor to travel to a named place. Visitor and place are both redacted. The trip is for talks on world banking needs. The talks would support work done for Soviet Bloc countries. The visitor was keen to take up the current foreign exchange troubles of the European Satellites. He wanted to gauge the rough size of the trade debt those countries owed Western banks. Their interest payments were part of the same point.

Swiss banks mattered greatly in the funding of East-West trade. Swiss bank secrecy had held back reporting from Switzerland. Guidance items cover Western European banks at work in Bloc trade finance. They cover loans to Bloc countries, and the security and interest terms on them. They cover Soviet Bloc gold sales, who handled them, and where the proceeds were held.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030013-0:
Agency requirements memo dated 17 December, with the year partly garbled in the scan, seeks facts on a redacted subject. The facts are to come through a named channel. They are due at the office by 20 January 1958. The background notes that Soviet Bloc civil defence had plainly been in active build-up for years. The scale and cost of that work might show Soviet intent, or Soviet fear of nuclear war. Full knowledge of Bloc civil defence systems could also help build short range warning signs.

Questions open with weapons facts. They ask what facts on modern weapons reach the public. They ask what reach mid-level civil defence officials and the central staff. They ask what accounts of nuclear attack effects are spread. Blast pressures, damage radii, and radioactivity levels and their span are all named. Later sections cover headquarters siting, communications, gear, and training.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030103-0:
Untitled Agency paper seeks progress reports on factory building in the eastern areas of the USSR. The projects are those listed in the directives of the Sixth Five-Year Plan. They are cited from a February 1956 gazette and a June 1956 Soviet press digest. Reports for any span should give planned and true ruble grants and spending, the labour force, and the supplies allotted and used. Cement, brick, and structural and reinforcing steel are named in particular.

Progress is to be measured in flat physical terms: cubic metres of digging, base pouring, roofing, and the fitting of plant gear. Problems in the work form a second head. They cover manpower gaps in hiring and keeping basic workers, skilled workers, and engineers. They cover supply gaps, by weight and by cause. They cover gear gaps, and poor use of the gear on hand.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180026-0:
Minutes ED/EC M-229 record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 2 April 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. They were issued on 8 April 1957. Mr. Hale chaired the meeting. An Agency member attended, with MDAC, Commerce, Defense, State, and Treasury. The agenda notes cover three items. One is an Agency paper on metalworking machinery. One is a summary of replies to a State circular. One is work program business left over from meeting No. 228.

Under the first note, the Agency member put in a short paper dated 2 April. The committee had asked for it at its last meeting. The paper covers the Sino-Soviet Bloc's supply position in metalworking machinery. The chairman tabled a secretariat draft summary of the circular replies. A State paper on the talks was expected soon. So the next meeting was set, for the time being, for 5 April. An EDAC meeting was set for 8 April.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180044-0:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-257, record a meeting at 10:00 a.m. on 18 July 1957. The meeting sat in Room 1213, Maiatico. The minutes were issued on 23 July 1957. The sole agenda head in the scan is quotas for China. Two sub-items under that head are redacted. State was to answer a Paris cable at once, saying Washington could not reply right away on one point. The point turned on bearings, and more study was needed.

Members were to check with their EDAC principals whether to go on with the item basis already put forward, or take up one of three other ways. A joint meeting with Working Group I was set for Friday, 19 July. Talk also weighed taking the problem to the Consultative Group, a step State opposed as a cause of delay. The group would not meet until September, and quotas should take effect at once.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180053-0:
Minutes ED/EC M-268 record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 4 September 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. They were issued on 10 September 1957. Mr. Hale chaired the meeting. ICA, State, Treasury, Defense, MDAC, the Agency, and Commerce were all at the table. A note covers fitness for aid, citing the EDAC D-136 series and EDAC M-63. The numbered item is the List II review for 1958.

On fitness for aid, the chairman spoke of EDAC D-136/5. That paper was being handed out that day. It reported an informal talk with the General Counsel. The talk covered questions raised at the last EDAC meeting. He stressed that the views in it were informal opinions only. On List II, talk weighed one point on Poland. Could Poland stay partly outside quota treatment for the rest of the year? Talk weighed how a single Bloc-wide quota would force item review on a Bloc basis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180062-0:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-276, record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 1 October 1957. The meeting sat in Room 913 of the District National Building. That was a change from the usual Maiatico room. The minutes were issued on 3 October 1957. A note covers the thermonuclear concept. Numbered items are the work program for paragraph 9 of economic defense policy. They are the embargo of copper wire, and List II quotas for 1958.

Commerce argued strongly on the first note. The next major joint meeting would face the thermonuclear concept one way or another. The United States should start getting ready to handle it now. That held whatever methods were worked out later. On quotas, State tabled a draft instruction to the United States delegation. It had been drawn after full review inside State. It set out EDAC level thinking on the point. State asked members to clear it with their principals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200010050-0:
Agency reference list dated 15 December 1954, marked For Official Use Only, is titled Government of the USSR. It opens with the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet. Kliment Efremovich Voroshilov is listed as Chairman, followed by a long list of deputy chairmen, a secretary, Nikolai Mikhailovich Pegov, and members, among them Nikita Sergeevich Khrushchev and Nikolai Mikhailovich Shvernik. Names are given in full with patronymics, in the order of the source.

Later pages list the ministries of the Soviet government by name. They run from defence industry and transport through radio technical industry, communications, machine tools, shipbuilding, heavy and medium machine building, chemical industry, electric power stations, and electric industry. The file is a ready reference sheet for staff who needed the current shape of the Soviet state apparatus.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200090043-0:
Correlation document in the Agency's files, dated November 1957, sets the current International Lists beside a proposed revision. The revision was put forward by the Ad Hoc Subcommittee on List Review. A table maps the numbering blocks of the lists. Metalworking machinery and related items sit in the 1000 to 1099 range. Chemical and petroleum gear sits at 1100 to 1199. Electrical and power gear sits at 1200 to 1299. General factory gear sits at 1300 to 1399. Transport gear sits at 1400 to 1499. Matching blocks run in the 2000 and 3000 series.

Item pages then work through single machines in fine detail. One family covers blade machines for aerofoil work. It lists edge radiusing, polishing, milling and grinding machines. It lists fillet radiusing, root milling, blank preforming, rolling, shaping, and scribing machines. Criteria letters are attached to each machine. The file is the working tool for setting old and proposed control lists side by side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130020-0:
Short paper dated 7 May 1957, an Agency ORR project numbered S-172, reports a push by Soviet military leaders. The leaders were urging increased civil defence efforts in the USSR. In April, both Pravda and Red Star carried accounts of a civil defence meeting of the Moscow Oblast Defence Group. Marshal Malinovsky, chief of the Soviet ground forces, addressed it, as did the DOSAAF chief and a major general earlier identified as a tank division commander. Names in the scan are partly garbled.

Speakers criticised DOSAAF and other organisations over civil defence training. The speakers called for wider civil defence work among the population. They called for wider use of retired and reserve generals as trainers. At popular level, civil defence training rested with DOSAAF. The Red Cross and Red Crescent societies handled first aid training. They handled preparation of medical auxiliaries as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130039-0:
Paper in the Agency's files takes up a decision of a Soviet Party plenum, reported in February 1957. Khrushchev addressed the plenum. The paper sees a sweeping reshaping of Soviet economic administration along regional lines as near. Khrushchev had noted overfulfilment of the 1956 plan. He had stressed the need for sharp improvement in factory planning and management to reach the 1960 goals. Weak points in the present system are underlined. The narrow approach of the factory ministries blocks joint work on the spot between plants of different industries.

The plenum decision goes past earlier half-steps, the paper holds. A new economic headquarters in each region will likely gain broad powers over economic activity there. Some central ministries may be reshaped, or even abolished. The decision does not say whether present republic capitals will house the new bodies, or whether fresh agencies will be created to run the reshaped regions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140083-0:
Study in the Agency's files, dated 23 April 1958 in the scan, takes up exports in Soviet Bloc foreign trade. It works through the export structure of the Bloc countries country by country. The USSR's trade pattern is set first, its shares of trade with the Bloc and the Free World compared, and China placed in the picture. Bloc trade with the Free World had grown, particularly since 1955. Trade with underdeveloped areas forms a growing part of the account, though still a minor share of Bloc totals.

A Czechoslovakia passage shows the factory shift in that trade. Czech exports of machinery and equipment had fallen to a low of 22 percent in 1953. Those are the paper's figures for that year. The goods form a heavy industry category. They recovered over the next three years under the post-Stalin program. By 1956 they reached about 43 percent of Czech exports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200200068-0:
Agency memo dated 1 April 1958, from the Chief, S/OM, to the Chief, D/S, reports the branch's work for March 1958. During March the branch submitted two branch projects, one briefing paper for the Director, and one current support paper. One branch project and two current support memoranda were published in the month. The Arctic Section briefed named officers on 7 March. It chaired the DD/I Group meeting on Soviet Arctic intelligence on 6 March, and supplied its executive secretary.

Submitted titles include Recent Management Measures to Promote the Industrial Development of Kazakhstan. They include Changes in Forced Labor Policy in the USSR. Briefing notes for the Director on Soviet civil defence, and a support paper on Soviet civil defence air raid drills, are listed as well. Published items include Soviet Civil Defense and Air Raid Shelter Construction and Reorganization of Communist China's Economic Ministries. Project time tables close the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200200077-0:
Agency memo dated 3 March 1958, from the Chief, S/OM, to the Chief, D/S, reports branch work for February 1958. During February the branch submitted three branch projects. It submitted three current support papers and three other support papers. Two current support papers and one short research paper were used for CID items and published. Titles show the branch's range that month.

Items include comments on a draft on forced labour in the USSR. They include Significant Northern Sea Route Activities. They include Soviet Civil Defense and Air Raid Shelter Construction. A paper on air raid shelter funds discussed by Soviet officials and an agenda for East German reorganisation are listed. Reorganization of Chinese Communist Economic Ministries appears as well. Papers on recent moves toward economic integration and coordination of the Soviet Bloc close the list. A closing note warns of a serious staff shortage in the branch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100020098-0:
Proposed joint operating procedure dated 3 March 1950 sets up a Permanent Committee on Soviet Capabilities and Intentions. The parties are the Central Intelligence Agency and the Departments of State, the Army, the Navy, and the Air Force. The committee is referred to in the text as the JACKPOT Committee. It would help the Agency produce and maintain coordinated estimates of Soviet capabilities and intentions.

Two ends are stated. The first is to let the most capable analysts of the four departments work with Agency analysts on all factors bearing on the Soviet question, against the widest regional and global background. The second end is to ensure the fullest use of member agencies' intelligence resources. Committee meetings rank ahead of any other duty of members. Special or emergency meetings may be called by the chairman, or at any member's request.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100090055-0:
Text of National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 16 covers foreign language materials. It assigns the Agency the central role in that field. Under the National Security Act of 1947, the Council gives one direction. The Agency will provide centrally the services of common concern. The services are exploiting, translating, and disseminating foreign language materials for intelligence. Certain material is excepted where the departments agreed to prepare it themselves for their own needs.

Departments and agencies have duties of their own under the directive. They will develop and maintain their own language facilities. They will maintain reference services for foreign materials. They will make available to the Agency all foreign language material that comes to them. Material agreed to be kept for their own departmental intelligence production is the exception. The Director of Central Intelligence is charged with ensuring the directive is carried out across the community.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100140167-0:
Document dated 1 June 1954, headed Agreed Activities, deals with clandestine operations run by the armed forces alongside the Agency. The opening pages are partly garbled in the scan, but the argument is legible in its main lines. There is a functional need, the paper states, for clandestine intelligence operations by the armed forces. The aim should not be to eliminate such operations, but to relate them properly to the Director of Central Intelligence, who holds primary responsibility in the field.

Later text ties the arrangement to NSCID No. 5. Military services may conduct exploitation operations as agreed activities under that directive's provisions, in order to promote the most effective use of capabilities and facilities available to the United States government. The paper works to fit service-run operations inside the Director's coordinating authority rather than outside it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000300150173-0:
Letter in the Agency's files, dated 26 July 1956, from Headquarters, Strategic Air Command, Offutt Air Force Base, Nebraska, to the Director of Intelligence, Headquarters USAF. It outlines how SAC would establish the TALENT Control System. It answers a request from Washington and includes the command's immediate requirement for clearance authorisation. The system would operate inside SAC under a TALENT Control Officer, supervised directly by the Director of Intelligence.

The Director of Intelligence, as senior intelligence officer of the command, would answer for the security and proper safeguarding of TALENT materials received at headquarters. A TALENT Control Officer and assistant, and a TALENT Security Officer and assistant, had been appointed to the duties the system prescribed. Later pages list cleared positions by directorate, including the Chief of the Mission Planning Group and analysts in the Radar Bombing Branch, each page marked for handling via the TALENT system only.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600030001-0:
A draft confidential memorandum dated 11 August 1955 circulates among State, USIA, naval, air, and Army intelligence offices. Its subject is intelligence material for a redacted place, tied to a survey of USIA needs. In April 1954 the heads of CIA and USIA had agreed that CIA staff would survey what intelligence USIA and related programs required. Member agencies and the Operations Coordinating Board took part.

One main result was an approved statement of need, listing the kinds of intelligence USIA required. That statement then grounded basic requirements for the National Intelligence Survey program. Staff tested it against two countries and built question lists for each. The memo reports that material gathered covered most questions asked. It still needed tailoring and editing, plus some fresh field reporting, before it would serve users well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600030010-0:
A secret memorandum dated 4 August 1955 goes to the Director of Central Intelligence with an organizational proposal. Its subject is production of intelligence on international communism. Output on communism plainly needed a large increase, the memo argues. That need had been voiced for years and restated in the USIA survey and in a board paper on propaganda against communism. Staff had been told to study where primary duty for this production should sit, in talks with State Department intelligence officials.

Three kinds of work need growth, the memo finds. Finished intelligence at a level useful to policymakers comes first. Other work is split between offices in the recommendations that follow. Some activity goes to the clandestine side. A third line, part intelligence, part estimate, and part policy speculation, should start with two or three senior officers. They would sit with the deputy directorate for intelligence while working closely with clandestine staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600070007-0:
Part II of a study on collection, dated 1 January 1955, defines what coordinating requirements means in practice. Before field collection counts as coordinated, several judgments must be made at headquarters. That duty falls on requirements officers in research offices and on staff close to collection managers. The first judgment asks whether the answer already exists in Washington, in finished intelligence or in files that skilled staff can locate.

Other judgments follow in turn. Staff must check whether a like requirement has gone out before, and whether each task matches its importance and the ability of the facility assigned. Bibliographies help with the checks. The paper cites the Library of Congress monthly list of Soviet publications, produced under contract, and steady work by the Foreign Documents Division. Priority lists under DCID 4/3 and 4/4 supply the most weighty statement of what matters most to national security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600150026-0:
Opening remarks by General Cabell, dated 28 August 1957, set up a briefing on Aquatone. The visit had two aims. First came a progress report on operations so far. Second came the problem of future missions. Cabell had lately asked the President for leave to fly certain missions. Their targets bore on guided missiles, atomic energy, and the Long Range Air Force. The answer was no.

Cabell feared the refusal rested on a missed point. In his view, the President had not taken aboard how weighty the open questions on Soviet work were. A later chance might let the Joint Chiefs or the Director press that case. The session plan followed: an Air Force colonel would lay out needs drawn from national estimates. The project director, Mr Bissell, would then report the current state of operations and what coverage could still be won.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700050026-0:
A status report on coordination projects opens with a stated problem: building sound ways to rank needs for the several collection units. First news concerns a new Interagency Priorities Committee. It will draft joined guidance for covert collection, chaired by one office, with the Agency's view carried by the coordination office. Members have built a list of thirty top geographic targets. They now seek a way to merge views into one government list of fifty.

Other entries follow the same pattern. An economic committee subgroup is ranking reporting needs, to guide State in running the Foreign Service reporting system. At G-2's request, CIA is listing needs that censorship records might meet. Later items weigh where duty for scientific intelligence should sit. One entry rethinks central handling of foreign language material: analyst language skills have grown, so a strong index plus translation on request may beat the present central system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070006-0:
A planning paper on using foreign intelligence materials opens with a shared worry: weak abstracting, reference tools, and control of publications. The issue had been raised under a draft NSCID 16 and during a review of open collection. Two needs stand out: getting material in, and making it findable under sound controls. A summary of the central reference arm's work follows.

That arm, OCD, has sought to serve CIA and the whole community. It claims the first use of central methods to sort, index, and spread intelligence papers in the United States system. Its shelves aim at full coverage in major languages, with pointers to holdings held elsewhere. Finding tools for secret papers match those scholars use in open work. Aids listed include an index to Soviet science prize winners for 1935 to 1951, studies of industrial sites, a library resources desk, and a monthly index of intelligence periodicals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470014-0:
Minutes of the thirteenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee cover a session held on 10 November 1955. They are dated 18 November. October minutes won approval at the start. Next came a revised paper on free world ship deliveries to the Sino-Soviet bloc in 1954. It also set out planned building at 1 July 1955.

The chairman said the paper would serve as useful background for a Washington intelligence conference set for 21 to 23 November. It would stand approved unless views arrived by 16 November. None did. A heavily withheld item follows in the record, after which members agreed to close Case 12. Talk then turned to rewriting the reporting rules on economic ties with the bloc. Later, members set up a working group on propellants and fuel additives. It replaced a group on magnesium. Its brief covers listed goods such as colloxylin and magnesium itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470023-0:
Minutes of the fourth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 10 January 1955. The group met on 21 December 1954. Its first topic was flow of facts from the military intelligence agencies. At the prior meeting, Commerce and the mutual defence office were asked to check their standing needs. The defence aid office had now lodged economic defence needs with all three services.

Commerce reported sound spread of such material at home. Its inquiry staff and the defence staff had set a direct line for enforcement facts. Yet the joint operating arm held that technical facts could beat raw intelligence when grading how strategic a good is. Talk also weighed seating a Commerce research voice on the committee itself. Later, members agreed that a paper going up should ask the intelligence community for its own grading.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100480059-0:
A second yearly progress report of the Intelligence Working Group covers 1 July 1953 to 30 June 1954. This copy is dated 1 September 1954. A contents page maps the whole: duties first, then work and wins, then chief problems and the program for the coming year. Six tabs close the report with lists and a chart.

The group's duties are stated plainly. It lines up intelligence resources and data for the Economic Defense Advisory Committee. It urges agencies to collect where gaps show. It also supplies both joined reports and fast spot facts. Tabs list every finished study and every information paper sent out.
