Further tabs list cases closed without a study, cases still open at 30 June 1954, and problems in gathering and using facts. A final chart shows how intelligence support for economic defence is wired.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100480068-0:
A second copy of the Intelligence Working Group's second yearly report fills the file, dated 12 August 1954. The period covered is the same: 1 July 1953 to 30 June 1954. Wording matches the known report in the main. Some pages in this copy are marked illegible. The group's duties open the text, in the same three parts.

Its forum role gets stress here. The group gives action agencies a shared table where they can draw on facts held across CIA, naval intelligence, and State's research arm. It thus acts as the working level hub of support for the parent committee. A footnote dates its birth: set up at the joint call of the Director for Mutual Security and the Secretary of State, with terms cleared 25 July 1952. The year ahead, the report adds, will be guided by policy paper NSC 152/3. War planning for economic warfare may also call the group into a fresh study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490021-0:
Minutes of the ninth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 4 May 1955. The group met on 28 April. The acting chairman first recalled a plan for watching freed goods. Three ways to gather facts had been floated: a direct approach to allied control partners, attaché reporting, and tapping defence aid contractors. Members had been asked to check their own shops.

The test was simple: did enough facts exist to merit a full study of bloc orders for all freed items? Commerce and State's research arm had extra tasks on a set of listed goods. Commerce sent a memo with trade figures on two list items, plus names of chosen electronics makers. It warned that trade tables lump goods into broad baskets, hiding single items. State offered a special gathering push on a few items of high weight.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510046-0:
A fifth yearly progress report of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee covers 1 July 1956 to 30 June 1957. It went to the Intelligence Advisory Committee on 25 October 1957 for noting. The committee closed its fifth year of work on 30 June. Its pace eased against earlier years, the report admits at the start.

A contents page maps the report. Program work fills the core: planning for economic warfare comes first. A full record of a propellants seminar held in June 1956 follows. Tabs list finished reports, other papers sent to members, and cases closed and pending. Future work keeps a sharp edge, the report states. The committee will keep hunting goods that grow in weight for the bloc as science and technique shift. It also waits for guidance from the mobilization office before fixing some lines of wartime planning work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510064-0:
A set of working rules for the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee is sent round, restated on 16 November 1955. The acting executive secretary signed the cover memo. The rules were first cleared in May 1953, under the group's old name. Small changes now bring names and titles up to date. Secretariat practice has also been tidied.

The attachment, restated on 16 November 1955, opens with roots. In August 1952 letters passed among the Director for Mutual Security, the Secretary of State, and the Director of Central Intelligence. With the Defence Secretary's backing, a working group was born. It later took the committee name used here. Its job is to back the Economic Defense Advisory Committee with intelligence. The rules call the body rare in government: it is both the hub of such support and the table where agencies join their work in the field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050082-0:
A goods study on magnesium, dated 6 April 1954, follows a set form for the joint operating body. It opens with a portrait of the metal. Magnesium is the lightest stable metal made in bulk. It is won by two routes, both hungry for electric power. At two-thirds the weight of aluminum, it pairs lightness with strength, easy cutting, and easy shaping at low heat.

Uses run wide. Alloys of it serve where light strength counts, above all in aircraft and transport gear. It enters aluminum alloys, aircraft engines and frames, radar and radio sets, and weapons. As powder it serves tracer rounds, fireworks, and flash powder. Making it well takes skilled chemists and metal men; the book facts are public, but hands-on craft cannot be swapped in. Output tables close the study, with French, Italian, and Norwegian figures. Italy's output, restarted in 1950, could reach 2,000 metric tons of capacity.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200100037-0:
A draft legal memo for the Director weighs what restricted data means for intelligence work. The term comes from the Atomic Energy Act. It covers all data on the design, making, or use of atomic weapons. It also covers making special nuclear material, and using it to make energy. Only the Atomic Energy Commission can free such data by declassifying it.

Two readings clash. CIA holds the act meant to guard data born inside the United States, where law can fence it from foreign hands. The atomic commission reads the words wider: all data on atomic topics, from any source, counts as restricted till it says otherwise. On that reading, every foreign fact CIA needs in the field falls under the act's bars till cleared. Later pages urge a way out: a ruling from the Attorney General that would bind the whole executive branch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070021-0:
A fat training file centres on a letter from Matthew Baird to Lawrence Houston. Baird ran training. A new test is under way in the Junior Officer Training Program. Rather than drip in across the year, a 1960 class will enter as one body in September. The class will take all its formal basic training together. Only then will offices take the young officers for work on the job.

Gains are listed with care. Idle gaps between courses end. Teaching can be tuned to one even group. Offices escape the pain of losing their trainees back to school mid-task. Language and area study will come when a need is shown, or, for clandestine work, once an overseas post is set. The formal course runs in six blocks. Baird asks Houston to speak in the first block, on the history of American intelligence. Schedules and aims ride along.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300080011-0:
A memo dated 9 January 1959 prices the Director's and Executive Dining Rooms. A study by two named staff sits behind it. Cost per meal, for regular, special, and official luncheons alike, ran to about ninety cents. That sum folds in spoilage, free meals for kitchen staff, salaries, laundry, heat, and lights. The Director had ruled the rooms serve a needed official task.

So overhead counts as a fair Agency charge, the memo holds. Two moves are urged. First, keep the member charge at one dollar a meal for all three kinds of luncheon. Second, drop the ten dollar overhead fee on official luncheons. Any loss the mess runs past what members pay would then fall on Agency funds. Concurrence notes from February add a rider: approval by the deputy director for support and by the Director. Later pages define an official meal: a foreign guest is usually present.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300110017-0:
An extract from a legal periodical digest kept by Agency counsel. It clips an article on military law from Pearl Harbor to Korea. The authors are Harold F. McNiece of St. John's law school and John V. Thornton of New York University. 

The digest pages weigh how far courts may reach into military justice. The Supreme Court, the authors argue, takes a narrow view of habeas corpus where servicemen are concerned. Humphrey v. Smith is cited for that stance. Lower federal courts, in turn, carry that broad due process stance into service cases. The writers side with the lower courts. In an age of large standing armies, they argue, a serviceman's rights should not be thinned by a tight grip on habeas review. Review of military commission rulings is treated as tightly held too, with Ex parte Quirin and the Yamashita case named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150004-0:
A memo for the record logs a manpower planning session held on 13 July 1959. The room mixed Agency men with White House staff, two civil service commissioners, and Budget Bureau men. Colonel L. K. White opened with the problem at hand. Age is spread badly across the Agency's middle and top grades. The Korean War build-up drew in a flood of young hires, and that wave is now bunched in the ranks.

White set two aims: lay out the problem, then hear what cures the guests might urge. A briefing on the mission and shape of CIA followed, then one on the raw numbers. Gordon Stewart drew the lessons out. The deeper the Agency digs, the less simple the fix looks, he warned. Talk turned to a bill that would grant power to realign the workforce.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150013-0:
A memo dated 21 January 1959 routes a draft savings order from the Director. The draft was built by a task force, the Inspector General, the personnel chief, and the General Counsel. The Inspector General had walked it through with the deputy director that same day. 

A note from the Inspector General explains those marks. They state the deputy's own views, he writes. In his eyes, the new text kills any risk of the order being read as a reduction in force. The task force's reach is widened too. His plan: retype it, let each man clear it with his own deputy, then walk it up through the deputy to the Director. The order itself is plain. All parts of the Agency must hunt real staff savings in the next eighteen months. Headquarters bulk is the chief target, though savings abroad count too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300220006-0: Declassified CIA minutes of the 16th publication board meeting. The publishers met. The file holds the minutes. The archive keeps the paper. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300230005-0:
A memo dated 19 February 1957 urges the Director to let go of the old OSS files. An aide writes that the wartime stock in CIA hands could one day shame the Agency. Tales drawn from it, by men free to mine it, might be laid at CIA's door though the acts were not its own. 

Send the files to the National Archives, the memo urges. There the public can read them with no tie to CIA. Only sheets that can never be shown would stay back. The stock is split three ways as things stand. In 1945 the State Department took most of the research and presentation branches' files. CIA got the rest through the Strategic Services Unit and the old CIG. Both shops have sent much on to the Archives since. The three holders keep some ninety per cent of the whole OSS mass.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050004-0:
A fat file holds the full pack on a plan to amend Order 10501. It opens with the same call for views, dated 10 October 1957 and signed by John S. Warner. His memo asks four top offices for word by mid-November. The aim: one joined Agency stance on the change.

The source mail rides whole in the pack. The Budget Bureau wrote to Director Allen Dulles. Under Order 10006, draft orders are sent round for views, it says. Three texts came with that call. The Attorney General's letter of 11 October 1957 heads the set. Next, the draft amendment to the 1953 order on guarding defense facts. Last, a draft note to the heads of all shops in the state. The Attorney General's letter, to Budget chief Percival Brundage, opens the case for change. Deep pages work the draft line by line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050013-0:
A short file pairs a sharp in-house warning with a letter to the Hill. The warning, dated 1 May 1958, is Houston's word to his own legal staff. At the May senior staff meet, General Cabell had aired a worry. As talk runs on, the veil slips, and plain secret facts pass by phone.

Time for a fresh drill, Cabell held, and Houston passes it on. Secret facts are not to pass by phone at all. Much work must still be done by phone, the note grants. If a point cannot be put in safe words, the delay of a face-to-face talk must be borne. The letter in the file goes to a House panel's counsel. It takes up a defense report on Soviet work, stamped for state use and never cleared with this Agency. Such a sheet, the letter argues, is a draft in truth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400060021-0:
A memo rules on an Army bid to ease the stamp on an old edict. The Army had asked that a clip from NIA Directive No. 5 drop to SECRET. One part of the clip counts most, the memo holds: the part that hands out spy and counter-spy work past the nation's shores. That part is why the old board set the text at TOP SECRET.

The ground has not moved since, the memo argues. Those same tasks now sit in a fresh text, NSCID No. 5, reworked as late as 15 September 1958. That text stands at TOP SECRET with tight spread, by the top council's own word. An old task sheet in the secret field is as hot as a fresh one. The deputy for coordination backs the line. Word should go back to the Army plain: the Agency is in no place to grant the drop.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400140004-0:
A study for the Headquarters Board of Survey restates when a staff man pays for state goods lost in his hands. It bites most in car crashes. Counsel took the study in hand to set the base rules out plain.

The root rule is one of fair care. A man must guard state stock as a sound, careful man would in his shoes. The care owed shifts with the facts in front of him and the kind of goods he holds. To give the rule teeth, the study turns to the law of bailment. That branch sorts the rights of an owner and of the man who holds his goods for a time. At one end stands a loan for the holder's sole gain. There the owner may claim the highest care of all. A slip, at that end, is enough to fix the bill on the holder.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100030003-0:
A RAND study, P-1540-RC of 10 November 1958, sets out trial work on political gaming. For four years, RAND's Social Science Division has run such games. The text tells how the play works. A list of RAND's loose notes on gaming rides at the back, for men keen to try the craft.

The roots run two ways. War games were old stock at RAND when the trial began. Some had tried to fold state craft into the play. One bold try was a cold war game with scores on each move. Moves could then be weighed by sums. That try was dropped. The sums called for a crude cut of real life, so deep that the game's worth for real state craft was in doubt. State games were also played in Japan before the last war, the team learned late.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100040020-0:
A memo gives point-by-point word on a survey of the tongue scheme. It goes to the chair of the tongue growth panel. His report of 25 August 1959 is praised in warm terms: a fine sum of gains to date, with sharp notes on the scheme's sore spots. The reply takes his points in his own order.

First comes the free study arm. Its fault: no firm goals, and a tail of men who gain no real skill. The fix, backed here in full: phase out the first-rung classes, the plain tongues first. Eight or nine of each ten weak men sit in just those classes. Ease of entry is blamed too. Hence a bar is set. A man must show a gift for tongues, or hold a base of skill, before he signs. The tongue he picks must have a clear use in his work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100040057-0:
A talk note logs a long gripe session on tongue school ties. Her theme: knocks on the school, heard at the top, are blown too large. The street runs two ways, she held.

On one side, the school can't get men out of the area shops to fill its classes. On the other, the shops say the school can't, or won't, shape its work to their true needs. Spain's tongue is the case in point. The West half shop will not free six men to make a class. A field note in the file cuts the same way from the far end. Two fresh men sent out to a post had no sound grip on the land's tongue. Full-time classes, the note adds, fill in a bare few tongues. French, German, and Greek are named among those with a steady flow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100110004-0:
Final reporting on Instructional Techniques Course No. 42 comes from its chief instructor in a 26 October 1959 report to the Director of Training. The class ran from 19 to 23 October 1959 for forty hours and drew seven students. All were instructors themselves, graded GS-11 through GS-14, drawn from courses run by the Operations Support Training Faculty.

Administrative detail covers the students' schooling, their present teaching posts, and support such as seven instructional films borrowed from a film library. A time analysis breaks the course into study periods, directed discussion, student presentations with class critiques, and film sessions. Each main topic, from lecturing to lesson planning, followed a set sequence meant to build teaching skill step by step.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100130048-0:
War and emergency planning inside the Office of Training is organised in a 14 May 1959 memorandum from the Director of Training to school and staff chiefs. Each intelligence body was expected to report plans for its own field to the Intelligence Board by 1 October 1959. Training could be asked for its contribution well before that date, so clear duties were needed at once.

The paper states the director's concept, fixes who holds planning duties at each level, and gives an outline to guide the work. A two-phase system splits action into steps taken before an emergency and steps taken after war begins. One named flaw in past Agency planning was weak part played by the operating officials who would carry plans out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200050006-0:
Changes agreed to the English text of the China Special List since document CH/170 was issued are gathered in Amendment Sheet No. 1, dated 30 November 1953. Each entry names the item affected and the authority for the change. Some entries only correct a single word, while others rewrite an item in full.

The largest rewrite covers item C-001, machine tools and their accessories, with exceptions for machines made for civilian hardware such as needles, pins, buttons, and nails. Portable hand-held power tools for metal work, mining, transport servicing, and other set uses are also redefined. A French version of the same amendment follows, so both language texts of the embargo list stayed in step.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200080003-0:
A full report by the chairman of the Sub-Committee on Export Controls covers its meetings of 26, 27, and 28 April 1960 for the Coordinating Committee. Delegates from member countries, from Belgium and Luxembourg to Japan, Turkey, Britain, and the United States, are named at the head. A contents list runs from approval of the agenda through diversions, import certificate procedure, and other enforcement business.

Diversion cases take up early sections, including Turkish borax and boron products, an attempted diversion of colemanite, Argentine borax watched in transit, and illegal shipments of ball bearings. Later pages work through how member states applied global import certificates, with Canada explaining that its licensing departments accepted certificates whether or not a quantity, value, or time limit was stated.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200110009-0:
Side-by-side comparison of export control definitions fills a study dated 22 July 1952. Selected items from the Japanese export control list are matched against the Coordinating Committee's China list and British supplemental items. This first part runs through item 13 of the Japanese list, laying the two sets of wording in facing columns so gaps show at a glance.

The opening Japanese item sweeps in all ferrous and non-ferrous ores, concentrates, metals, alloys, and scrap. Matched entries include iron powder of very fine grain and munitions components such as brass fabrications for bullet cups, cartridge belt links, and primer caps. Later items treat graphite electrodes, natural graphite crucibles, and sulphur in its crude, ground, refined, and sublimed forms. The comparison let officials see where Japanese wording ran wider or narrower than allied lists.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200050011-0:
Work finished by the Geography Division during December 1958 is listed in a memorandum dated 7 January 1959. Report numbers, project numbers, titles, classifications, and requesters fill the table. National Intelligence Survey chapters appear for North Korea and Sweden, along with map and chart appraisal work tied to survey chapters.

Antarctic subjects stand out among the finished pieces. One study weighs the shadow of possible cold war tensions in Antarctica, and another covers the Soviet Union's fourth Antarctic season. A geographic brief on a Soviet economic region also appears. Scheduled work listed at the end includes a study of grain production in Communist China, showing the division's queue reaching well beyond maps.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00865r000200280002-0:
Seventeen life sketches of Viet Minh leaders were finished on 19 March 1954. The sketches study their training in world communism. The opening claim is blunt. North Vietnam called itself a home-grown freedom movement. Yet the sketches say twelve of its seventeen top leaders were trained by the Comintern. Their training took place in Moscow, Paris, Yenan, or Canton, some as early as 1920.

Ho Chi Minh is treated first, as the leading figure. He is placed in France and the Soviet Union from 1911 to 1925. He attended early meetings of the Third International. In China in 1925 he worked as a translator for the Comintern agent Borodin. Later sketches cover a top labour leader. They also cover Hoang Van Hoan, the republic's first envoy to China and a party leader.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000100090027-0:
Field offices of the Contact Division come under inspection in a partial, preliminary report dated 9 November 1953, written for the Inspector General. The writer inspected offices and resident agencies of the Contact Division, part of the Office of Operations, between 6 September and 23 October 1953. A full report covering the whole office would follow later.

His method is described in detail. He went through a set list of questions with each office chief, dictated the results, then interviewed every staff member separately and in private, typing the interview reports himself. A second talk with the chief closed each visit. Findings touch how field offices judged their sources, with complaints that model reports sent from headquarters were stronger in form than in intelligence content.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000200010015-0:
More comments on the Inspector General's survey of the Technical Services Staff reach the Director of Central Intelligence on 8 July 1958. The survey had made one hundred sixty points for change. An earlier paper from the plans directorate had proposed action on one hundred forty-one of them. This paper deals with the rest.

Action on fourteen points was to wait for word from overseas posts. Five more were put off. Two of those five had since been covered by a January 1958 paper. The detail sits in attachments. One is a memo from the chief of the staff surveyed. Sixteen more attachments take seventeen points one by one. Each states the action the Director was asked to approve.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000200010033-0:
Comments from the plans directorate on the Inspector General's survey of the Technical Services Staff are forwarded on 7 August 1957 by Frank G. Wisner, Deputy Director for Plans. The Inspector General's report held one hundred forty specific recommendations. For each one, an attachment quotes the recommendation, states the action the directorate proposed, and gives the reason behind that proposal.

A summary groups the proposed outcomes. Some items were put forward for approval as written, others for approval with changes or limits, and others for no action at all. Further items were deferred until overseas comments arrived, postponed, or marked for disapproval. A separate tab gathers general comments on the survey from the chief of the staff that had been surveyed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040019-0:
Comments on an Inspector General report about the Personnel Office open by calling its analysis generally sound. The report showed the Agency's broad personnel management problems clearly. It also exposed the general confusion over divided duties and authority for personnel work, named here as the basic cause of many flaws in the Agency's personnel program.

One weakness in the report itself is noted: a reader cannot easily tell which flaws the Personnel Office could fix on its own and which belonged to other authorities. The comments argue that the office head should give expert advice and central services and watch the program for the Director, while operating supervisors handle day-to-day personnel work. Quoted findings on placement officers follow, faulting their grasp of the skills that open posts required.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500080006-0:
An Inspector General survey of the Assessment and Evaluation Staff in the Office of Training opens with its table of contents and purpose. The inspection was made at the request of the staff's own chief, with the training director's agreement. A push by an Efficiency Task Force to cut staff personnel by twenty-five per cent had raised questions the survey was meant to help settle.

Four branches structure the staff's work: a testing service and administration branch, an assessment branch, a training evaluation branch, and a research branch. Major problems take up the second half, covering Agency policy and ties with other components such as the Medical Staff and the Clandestine Services. One problem discussed is how supervisors should help staff move into wider fields instead of blocking their ambition.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200010039-0:
Deployment of an AQUATONE detachment to the Far East is urged in a memorandum to the Chief of Staff of the United States Air Force, dated 15 November. Talks between the Agency and the Air Force had left two questions open: when the detachment should go, and which theatre base best balanced political and operational needs. A survey group with Agency and Air Force members had toured the region to inspect facilities.

Half the survey group had returned and reported, and the Far East Air Forces commander had reported as well, so the writer argues the open issues can now be settled. Early local flying would build familiarity with the area and sharpen readiness before spring weather improved. A ready capability in place could also meet needs raised by sudden events in the region.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200060034-0:
Longer-run choices for Project AQUATONE are framed in a draft memorandum dated 7 May 1956. Time was drawing near, the paper argues, for basic decisions on the project's ultimate future. One question asks how long the project should run inside its present organisation. A second asks how this clandestine gathering activity should be organised for the long term.

Practical planning turns on the answers. Sums for the fiscal year 1958 budget, the length of service needed from Agency, Air Force. Contractor staff, disposal of the project's facility, and how far equipment development should go all wait on them. The Air Force's own plans and the likely span of the present arrangements are weighed as background, and the writer closes with a personal outline of the likely course ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200130036-0:
Keeping Project CORONA secret in 1960 is weighed in a March 1959 paper. The paper is tied to a plan for eight more flights that year. The 1959 flights were to be hidden under the public DISCOVERY series. One choice is to hide the 1960 flights the same way. The other is to name them openly, inside the armed services, as a separate spy flight project. A public notice of the true task would come in due course.

That choice is called mainly a foreign policy one. Two checks are still needed first. One asks how well secrecy can hold through a second year. The other asks what a public notice on 1960 would do to the 1959 program. All concerned knew how vital secrecy was. But the paper warns that defence staff and outside advisers would be sure to guess that such a secret program existed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00101a000100120032-0:
Needs for an electronic spy operation are sent round by the Committee on Overhead Reconnaissance on 7 September 1960. The paper is numbered COMOR-D-6. It resends a basic needs paper agreed by the committee's earlier body on 1 June 1959. The resending is for the committee's own use and ready reference. The paper could be taken up again later if the need arose.

Copies go across the spy community. Army, Navy, and Air Force spy arms all receive it. So do the National Security Agency, the State Department, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The needs paper looks ahead to sharper target lists. Lists tied to top needs would be drawn up with the Pacific Air Forces. The Pacific Command's own needs group would help. A processing centre would then add detail, starting with the known facts on radars.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100020075-0:
Soviet electric motor production is captured in dense data tables for three-phase induction motors up to one hundred kilowatts. Columns give each model's power in kilowatts, speed in revolutions per minute, net weight in kilograms, and price in rubles. Model codes run through the table in groups, with suffixes marking different frame and speed variants.

Notes after the tables explain the groupings. Group A and Group B cover the standard enclosed forms, Group C covers enclosed and ventilated models. Group D covers shorted-rotor shielded multi-speed machines for two hundred twenty, three hundred eighty, and five hundred volts. Cast-iron casing series and dual-speed options at seven hundred fifty and fifteen hundred revolutions per minute are also noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050009-0: An annex of priority targets lists installations, locations, and background information in table form, but almost every entry in the released copy is blacked out. Column headings for installation, location, and background information repeat across the pages, with only a fragment of legible content surviving. One visible fragment concerns missile guidance components for a surface-to-air missile system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110084-0:
Key points from the Industrial Division are listed for a half-year report to the President's Board of Consultants. Work on economic facts comes first. The research office gave strong help to a national estimate on main trends in Soviet strength and policy, 1958 to 1963. Its help bore most on the Soviet long-range strike force, now and as projected.

An East German survey section on making and building had been finished. A paper on Soviet army and economic spending from 1955 to 1963 went to member agencies. It was used to brief Congress, the National Security Council, and the Secretary of Defense. The Army Policy Council was briefed too. A second half names big gaps in knowledge. The gaps are led by bloc army gains and by spending on missiles, planes, and submarines.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110129-0:
January 1959 work is reported in an Industrial Division monthly report dated 3 February 1959. A senior office asked urgently for a paper. The paper dealt with a Khrushchev statement of 27 January. It asked what the statement implied for missile output. The study took as given that series output of the missiles began in early January 1959. On that base it weighed Soviet power to make and field the missiles through mid-1962.

A branch chief briefed the spy directorate on gains since his branch grew a year before. That talk led to a full review of the branch's task, work, and staff. A formal request also came from the SR Division. It asked for close target studies of chosen missile sites in the Soviet Union. The research office took up the job jointly with the current facts office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110138-0:
Where bloc economic study sits, and why it matters, is set out in a short paper. Sound judgment of these closely linked economies needs one joined research effort. Other spy arms are not set up for bloc-wide economic work. They are not charged with it either. By joint agreement, and by a directive from the Director, the main duty rests with the Office of Research and Reports.

In 1957 the focus fell on the steadiness of the bloc. The shocks in Eastern Europe in late 1956 drove that choice. Studies probed what might stir more unrest in the satellites. Work on methods also features. A costing method built over two years for Soviet army programs was being widened. Getting the most from a steady flow of facts takes slow, costly effort, the paper notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120010-0:
December 1959 activity fills an Industrial Division monthly report dated 6 January 1960. Senior staff briefed the Director of Central Intelligence on a national estimate of Soviet capabilities for strategic attack through the mid-1960s, finished by month's end. Members of the intelligence board were also briefed on general economic developments, with weight on military expenditures under another estimate covering Soviet capabilities and policies from 1959 onward.

A Khrushchev statement in Budapest on 1 December about missiles brought requests for comment and support to a current intelligence publication. Analysts at a field site passed word that a substantial number of Soviet citizens of German origin had lately reached West Germany, and the home office was alerted at once. Support work for the 1959 review of the international strategic trade list is also recorded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120047-0: August 1959 work is reported in an Industrial Division monthly report. The scan is badly garbled. Only part of it can be read with confidence. Clear items include talks with another agency on an outstanding collection need. A project on Soviet missile systems is also named. A survey section on making and building in East Germany is named too. That section was the first from the research area to win a top quality rating. The report records the point with pride.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130073-0:
Talking points prepared around a visit by the Soviet Minister of Aviation and his delegation size up Soviet air power bluntly. First, the long-range force is equipped mainly with medium-range aircraft that would normally need refuelling for strikes against the United States. Second, the Soviets have built only a token heavy bomber force, with no signs of intent to increase it soon.

Third, the Soviets have yet to produce a supersonic all-weather fighter in any quantity. Fourth, Soviet military air transport has progressed little beyond the American C-47 stage, and new transport programs move slowly. Lead times draw special interest: the scientific intelligence office had tried hard to estimate them, so remarks by Mikoyan and Dementiev mattered. The Bull bomber's short lead time is explained as a direct copy of the American B-29.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130082-0:
Review copies of a gaps statement on the East German aircraft industry are forwarded on 13 February 1959 by the Aircraft Branch. The statement's background repeats why the industry matters: its scope, actual performance, and progress carry strategic and economic weight for the United States. The money and effort spent on aircraft production can indicate East German and Soviet intentions at home and abroad.

The questions that follow show what was still unknown. Is a named German design the last East German entry in a Soviet-bloc trainer competition? How many '152' aircraft will be built? When will the first aircraft meant for airline use roll from the factory? Have major problems developed in the program? The gaps format turns scattered reporting into a direct shopping list for collectors.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100160016-0:
Facts wanted on Soviet army programs are issued in a paper dated August 1959. The items sit in two parts, in order of rank. The first part backs the costing of army programs in the Soviet Union. Such cost work rests on fine detail about set programs. The items are framed to draw that detail out of reporting lines.

The second part is looser. Its items matter only for the broad kind of facts they might bring in. They are not tied to any single costing. Copies of the paper run to the research branches. Those branches work on Soviet army costs. The paper thus shows how a standing wish list steered collection. It steered it toward the figures the cost men lacked most.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100010014-0:
Economic intelligence is defined and its tasks laid out in a training text. Economics, the text begins, is the science of production, distribution, and use of wealth, the material means of satisfying human wants. Competition for a share of the world's resources has been a major cause of war, and economic weapons are accepted means of international conflict short of direct military action.

Economic potential is called the best single measure of a nation's strength. The analyst's study of a specific country reveals the location and character of steel plants, freight yards, oil refineries, power stations, and chemical plants. It also reveals industrial bottlenecks, and the degree to which military effort would be hampered by the loss of particular materials or facilities. A set of questions follows for assessing the factors that make up a country's economic potential.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100020112-0:
Procedures for starting and reviewing research projects in the Economic Research Area are laid down in Procedures Instructions No. 2, dated 23 July 1958, issued by the Central Intelligence Agency's Office of Research and Reports. All research projects need the approval of the Chief of Economic Research. For small support projects, that authority is delegated to division and staff chiefs, who may pass it further to branch chiefs.

A branch starting a project outside the annual program prepares a Project Initiation Memorandum in the form attached. If the new project will delay a scheduled one, the memorandum must say so in a set sentence. Projects are classed by type: an Office of Research and Reports publication, work for the National Intelligence Survey, work for a national estimate, or other.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040093-0:
A run of letters from November and December 1959 carry the same enclosure. Several of the letters survive in more than one copy. The enclosure is the Director's statement to a Joint Economic Committee group. It deals with economic statistics. It was delivered on 13 November 1959. The notes call the talk the Agency's latest thinking. The theme is United States growth set against Soviet growth.

The talk is also said to show the close tie between spy work and policy. It shows a good deal about the kind of economic research done in the Agency. One writer thanks his host for a fine visit to the campus the month before. He offers, in return, open papers that might help the host's own research. That research deals with the Soviet economy. Names and addresses are blacked out in this cleaned release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040200-0:
Views of the Economic Research Area on pre-publication coordination of research papers are sent to the Economic Intelligence Committee on 31 July 1959. The question is whether a number of the area's reports should be routed through the appropriate committee subcommittees before publication. The memorandum grounds itself in the directive defining the committee's coordination duties for foreign economic intelligence.

The answer is largely no. Division chiefs and senior officers were unanimous in disagreeing with any attempt to coordinate virtually all other area projects through the subcommittees. The main reason is a lack of competence among the majority of subcommittee members for that work. Where real individual competence exists, as with rocket fuels or census work on population and manpower, informal coordination already happens as normal practice, the paper argues.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090025-0:
Psychological warfare as practised by the Communist world is the assigned subject of an address by Allen W. Dulles to the Women's Forum on National Security, in Washington on 30 January 1959. The title is 'The Communist Challenge to Free Government.' The forum was held under the auspices of the American Legion Auxiliary.

Dulles jokes that the Soviet type of psychological warfare bears little resemblance to the kind his audience is reputed to employ. The body of the speech lists Communist front groups and their reach. In student and youth affairs, influence runs through the World Federation of Democratic Youth. It is called a major Communist front. It claims eighty-six million members in ninety-six countries. It works closely with the International Union of Students. Their joint output is described: two major publications in eleven languages, hundreds of pamphlets, and a steady flow of propaganda aimed at the young.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090034-0:
Comments on a speech by Mr. Staats are recorded in a memo dated 22 October 1959. The speech is titled 'National Security and Economic Growth.' The writer is the Chief of the Economic Research Area. The comments were given by word of mouth that afternoon. They went to Mr. Carey of Mr. Staats' office. The writer believes Mr. Carey accepted all of them, for a new form of the October 14 draft.

The speech text is attached to the file. It begins by widening the term national security. The term is stretched beyond direct army programs. It covers the total stance of the United States against the varied challenge of Communism. Later pages wrestle with Soviet figures. Even the spy community leans over backward, the speech notes, to stress that the official Soviet budget cannot be taken at face value. The meaning of single sums can only be guessed at from comparisons.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090052-0:
Communist Economic Penetration of West is a declassified Agency briefing outline on Soviet trade and aid as a new policy tool. It notes that Soviet trade with poorer free world nations had risen over 500 percent since 1954. Total Soviet trade with the West had more than doubled in the same span.

The outline describes joint reporting by State, the Agency, and other departments every two weeks since February 1956. It rates Soviet output as second only to that of the United States. Country cases follow, among them Yugoslavia, India, and Egypt. Each case shows aid timed to a local need, such as steel plans in India or a cotton surplus in Egypt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090089-0:
The Soviet Economy is a declassified Agency lecture text tracing Soviet growth from a farm economy to the second largest economy in the world. It credits forced industrial growth under Stalin, with heavy industry first. Under Khrushchev, the stated aim became catching and passing the United States in output per person.

Figures track that race across the years. Soviet gross national product is put at 33 percent of the United States level in 1950 and 39 percent in 1958. A share of about 47 percent is projected for 1962. Later sections turn to farming, where long neglect held down living standards for a growing population.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090124-0:
Communist Economic Penetration is a short declassified Agency outline on Soviet trade and development aid. It quotes Khrushchev's line that against the slogan of arms, Moscow replies with the slogan of trade. Soviet trade with poorer areas is reported up 500 percent since 1954.

The outline sizes up Soviet strength and its limits. Total Soviet output topped that of Britain, France, and West Germany combined, yet trade stayed small beside output. Most Soviet trade still stayed inside the Bloc. Credit terms close the outline: interest near two and a half percent, payment starting once a plant ran, and a twelve year span to repay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100005-0:
A statement by Allen W. Dulles, Director of Central Intelligence, to a subcommittee of the Joint Economic Committee of Congress on 13 November 1959 anchors this declassified Agency text. Its subject is how the Soviet and United States economies compare. Dulles notes that views on that question ranged from Soviet backwardness to a galloping giant.

He describes the Agency's work on the problem as broad and weighed without bias. Experts inside and outside government advised on fields from farming to advanced military goods. The statement grants that Soviet industry surged forward from 1928 to 1958 at a pace past that of the United States. It adds that Soviet growth built on technical ground the West had pioneered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100050-0:
The Challenge of Soviet Power is an address by Allen W. Dulles, Director of Central Intelligence, to the Edison Electric Institute in New Orleans on 8 April 1959. Dulles notes that Lenin defined Communism as the Soviet system plus electrification. The first Soviet economic plan of the early 1920s put a modern electric power system among its chief goals.

Much of the address compares output in the two systems. Soviet primary energy output is put at 45 percent of the United States level in 1958, rising close to 60 percent by 1965. The gap in steel had been shrinking for five years. Dulles cautions his audience not to rest on the idea that the absolute gap must keep growing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020013-0:
Comments on CFEP Drafting Group Staff Study No. 1, dated 21 June 1955, review a study on the aims and tests for controlling trade with the Soviet Bloc. The reviewer praises its treatment of past and present control policy. Its talk of tests for judging controls is called sharp and full of promise.

Criticism follows at equal length. The study is judged narrower than its title, since it deals almost wholly with a numbers method for raising the long-run cost that controls impose on the Bloc. The reviewer asks whether long-run cost alone can measure a control system. Notes on Soviet gold sales as a large scale practice round out the page by page remarks. The comments survive in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100040002-0:
Foreign Attitudes Toward Economic Defense is Staff Study No. 3 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review, draft of June 6, 1955. The study runs to 31 pages in this copy. Its abstract holds that foreign attitudes must count as a first concern in any talk of curbing trade with the Soviet Bloc.

Country sections give that claim its weight. The Italy section notes profits some traders drew from illegal trade in strategic goods. Legal trade, it warns, would leave Italian firms facing high production costs in Eastern Europe. Large United States aid is named as one reason Italy might still follow the United States lead. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100110004-0:
Use of Inducements or Pressures on Free World Countries in Support of the U.S. Economic Defense Program is Staff Study No. 11 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of May 20, 1955. It lists methods, some already in use, for drawing free world nations behind United States trade controls. A caution opens the study: a method unfit for one problem may still suit another.

Cases ground the catalog in real places. Aid work in the Helmand Valley of Afghanistan shows help used as an inducement. A further case suggests that buying chromium for the United States stockpile could improve Turkish help in denying borax to unfriendly nations. Each method is weighed for fit rather than praised outright. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100120003-0:
Economic Penetration of Underdeveloped Areas by the Communist Bloc is Staff Study No. 12 of the CFEP Drafting Group, dated June 1, 1955 and contributed by the State Department. Its stated problem is direct: what should the United States do when poorer nations accept Soviet Bloc offers of trade and development aid?

Later pages describe the Soviet machinery for such aid. Technopromexport, the Soviet export body named in the study, could sign all kinds of deals abroad. Its tasks ran from shipping gear to overseeing assembly and putting plants into operation. Training foreign workers, both in the USSR and abroad, formed part of its charge as well. The paper rests in the Agency's CREST release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100140001-0:
Enhancing the Effectiveness of CG/COCOM/CHINCOM is Staff Study No. 15 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 6, 1955. It poses one question: how should the United States raise the unity and strength of the joint bodies that run security trade controls? Those bodies are named in its title.

The study argues that a shared doctrine comes first. All partner nations needed a basic set of beliefs they could accept, strong enough to hold the control system together. The Consultative Group itself is judged sound and now set on a long-haul basis. It should no longer be treated as a short term, informal committee, the study concludes. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160009-0:
U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls is Staff Study No. 16 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 7, 1955. Section one lays out COCOM enforcement and the understandings on which primary controls over strategic exports rested. Partner nations held the first duty to police shipments from their own ports.

A later section lists why enforcement lagged. Hopes for coexistence, the study argues, cooled allied zeal for the whole control program with time. Some nations would not adopt enforcement steps unless all partners did the same. Others stressed trade promotion over trade control, and in some nations the controls themselves were kept secret, which hampered open enforcement. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200100022-0:
An enclosure in declassified Agency files, numbered CA-4148, presents Diversion Control Panel Case 394. It concerns 30,000 tons of Chilean copper and the International Trading Corporation of Seattle. A Wellington telegram of 14 September 1955 reports that the firm sought help from a New Zealand firm, J. L. Lennard Ltd.

The copper was to sail for Shanghai, with the ship chartered in London and payment on arrival. The Seattle firm admitted the United States Treasury had warned it that such a deal was illegal. It thus sought a partner in a nation with weak controls. A second case in the enclosure covers 2,000 tons of copper priced at 1,970,000 dollars, routed in transit toward Switzerland.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040066-0:
Final Course Report, Instructional Techniques Course No. 43, reports a forty hour course held from 28 March to 1 April 1960. Five students took it in the TSD Conference Room. All were photographic staff at grades GS-9 through GS-12 whose duties required them to teach others.

A time breakdown shows where the hours went. Student presentations and class critique took the largest share, just under half the course. Directed discussion and study periods took most of the rest, with films and their discussion a small tail. Two students held bachelor degrees. Seven films from the training library backed the lessons on learning, planning, and speech. The report survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020012-0:
Language Development Program is an Agency regulation, revised 8 December 1958, that sets the rules for building language skill across the Agency. Foreign language training could be taken as an assigned duty, as a voluntary off-duty pursuit, or as a mix of both. Training was free to the individual in each case.

Money awards form the program's spur. Staff who reached and held set levels of skill in awardable languages, proven by test, earned payment for their effort. Exclusions guard the scheme's intent. No award goes for skill gained chiefly by living abroad or through family ties. Skill kept up by the job itself, with no real effort, is likewise barred.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020102-0:
Review of Training Programs is a memorandum dated 29 April 1960 from the Chief, Plans and Policy Staff, to the Director of Training. It rests on a USIB memorandum by General C. P. Cabell of 5 April 1960. Cabell had noted that no community review or formal coordination covered the separate training efforts of the intelligence agencies.

An OTR staff meeting on 9 April took the point up. Supervisors were urged to review their own work on a set cycle and to start fixes ahead of outside pressure. A mid text list shows the sort of steps already taken. Basic country survey courses were cut back to the USSR alone. Orientation briefings were given on demand. Language testing was stepped up. The memorandum survives in the Agency's CREST files.
doe-osti-2997150-the-tranft-user-manual-:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229007-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-142, is version 2.0 of the user manual for TRANFT, by M. Blaskiewicz. TRANFT is a simulation code for the Electron-Ion Collider project that follows particles around a storage ring turn by turn. Its main worry is coherent instability, where a beam's particles start moving together in ways that can wreck the beam.

The manual lays out the theory first: single particle updates for energy and arrival time, transverse motion with chromatic effects, radiation damping, and random quantum kicks. A new algorithm in this version models the transverse voltage of crab cavities, including several feedback loops. Users choose how many updates happen per turn, trading speed against detail. Ring designers studying stability limits get both the physics and the operating instructions in one place.
doe-osti-3002284-the-viskores-user-s-gui:
Kenneth Moreland wrote a full software manual, The Viskores User's Guide, release 1.0, dated July 23, 2025. Viskores is a library that simplifies writing parallel scientific visualization code. It handles the distribution of work across processors, so developers can focus on the visualization itself. A comparison in the guide shows its marching cubes code far shorter than the reference CUDA version.

The guide runs to hundreds of pages in five parts. Early chapters cover building, installing, and a quick start. Middle parts document data sets, file input and output, and the provided filters, from contouring to slicing. Later parts treat rendering, error handling, device management, and timers. An index closes the volume. It is a reference for programmers building visualization tools on supercomputers, not a narrative report.
doe-osti-3030010-crada-final-report-crad: Agriwater got CRADA-finalled NFE-22-09311, and this DOE final reports the tech. The pages detail the number findings. The industry folks get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was industry. The 09311 were NFE-22. The Tech were Agriwater. The closeout were industry.
doe-osti-3363062-calderacast-user-manual: CalderaCast got manual-1.0'd, and this DOE text guides users version 1.0. The pages detail the findings. The computing folks get their data. The manual was user. The data were computing. The 1.0 were version. The user were manual. The computing were data.
doe-osti-3827267-geowise-user-manual-1-0: GeoWISE got 1.0-manualed, and this DOE manual covers the user manual. The pages detail the GeoWISE findings. The researchers get their data. The manual was 1.0. The data were researcher. The GeoWISE were manual. The 1.0 were researchers. The manual were user.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
In the Fire of the Forge reaches Volume 2 with Georg Ebers deep in old Nuremberg, his romance of knights and merchant families. Ebers gives the morning to Eva Ortlieb, who has not slept at all. She slipped out at dawn to dress in the next room without waking her sister Els, and hurried her maid through every step for once in this volume.

Chapter V explains her haste through the thoughts she carried to her prayer stool. Eva is certain her patron saint led the knight Heinz Schorlin to her, and that he is hers to command. She means to use that power well: to draw him from worldly vanity and make him a fighter for the Church. Sky blue, the Virgin's color, will be her color and his. Piety and first love here wear the same dress.
podcast-joerogan-J-CQjxKFb_0:
Nature writer Rowan Jacobsen joins Joe Rogan for episode 2516. Jacobsen writes books on oysters, forests, and wild food. His work links taste with ecology in plain prose.

Rogan, a keen hunter and eater, meets him on shared ground. They talk about how wild places feed both body and mind. Jacobsen shares tales from coasts, woods, and farms. The episode is a green, curious hour. It suits listeners who love the outdoors and want to know how food webs hold together, from tide pool to table. Each story ties a meal back to a place.
podcast-joerogan-_UduwgMDR-0:
Missing-persons researcher David Paulides brings his cases to episode 2502 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Paulides, a former detective, runs the CanAm Missing project, which logs strange vanishings in wild places. His books argue the cases share patterns no one has explained.

He tells Rogan about the newest files: skilled outdoorsmen gone near water or boulders, searches that find nothing, and finds that make little sense. Rogan asks what Paulides himself thinks is taking people. The episode is a chilling catalogue of the unexplained, from a methodical collector who insists he only reports the pattern.
podcast-joerogan-c-313sIpL_0:
Scientist Shanna Swan joins Joe Rogan for episode 2476. Swan studies how chemicals in plastics and goods affect human fertility. Her book Count Down warns of falling sperm counts.

She lays out data on a drop she calls a crisis. Rogan asks what in daily life drives the change. Swan names common products and the chemicals they shed. She also shares what people can do to cut risk. The episode is sobering and clear. It suits listeners who want a grave health claim argued with care by its lead researcher. Parents will read her warnings with care.
